claims.population: Patients with established vascular disease or high-risk diabetes without heart failure — older and sicker than an AAS-using population by a wide margin
claims.quote: Telmisartan was equivalent to ramipril in patients with vascular disease or high-risk diabetes and was associated with less angioedema. The combination of the two drugs was associated with more adverse events without an increase in benefit.

claims.statement: Across the ARB class as a whole, the evidence does not support declaring a winner. Newer ARBs including telmisartan look better than losartan and valsartan on BP reduction in some trials, but the reviewer's overall verdict is that the evidence is insufficient for definitive conclusions — so 'telmisartan is the best ARB' overstates what is known.
claims.dose: none
claims.population: Adults with essential hypertension across published randomised comparative ARB trials
claims.quote: Overall, there is insufficient weight of evidence to allow definitive conclusions to be drawn regarding the comparative efficacy of the available ARBs. However, newer ARBs (e.g. olmesartan medoxomil and telmisartan) appear to be more effective than older ARBs (e.g. losartan and valsartan) in reducing DBP and/or SBP in some trials.

claims.statement: There is a concrete, non-customary reason to favour renin-angiotensin blockade specifically in this population: AAS-associated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. In a series of 10 bodybuilders with proteinuria (mean 10.1 g/day) and renal insufficiency, seven received RAS blockade alongside stopping AAS, and creatinine stabilised or improved with reduced proteinuria. The authors also warn that creatinine is systematically hard to interpret in this group because of muscle mass.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the paper reports 'renin-angiotensin system blockade' as a class without naming agents or doses; agent and dose require a prescriber assessing renal function and proteinuria
claims.population: 10 bodybuilders (6 white, 4 Hispanic; mean BMI 34.7) with biopsy-proven FSGS after long-term anabolic steroid abuse
claims.journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology
claims.quote: Among eight patients with mean follow-up of 2.2 yr, one progressed to ESRD, the other seven received renin-angiotensin system blockade, and one also received corticosteroids. All seven patients discontinued anabolic steroids, leading to weight loss, stabilization or improvement in serum creatinine, and a reduction in proteinuria.

claims.statement: Hard-outcome data, not surrogates: in 1,189 Danish men sanctioned for AAS use followed ~11 years against 59,450 matched controls, cardiomyopathy risk was ~9-fold, heart failure ~3.6-fold, MI ~3-fold and VTE ~2.4-fold higher. This is the reason BP control matters here rather than being cosmetic.
claims.dose: Real-world illicit AAS use; doses not captured by the registry
claims.population: 1,189 men sanctioned in an antidoping programme in Danish fitness centres 2006–2018 vs 59,450 age- and sex-matched general-population controls
claims.quote: AASs were associated with an increased risk of acute myocardial infarction (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 3.00 [95% CI, 1.67-5.39]), percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass graft (aHR 2.95 [95% CI, 1.68-5.18]), venous thromboembolism (aHR 2.42 [95% CI, 1.54-3.80]), arrhythmias (aHR 2.26 [95% CI, 1.53-3.32]), cardiomyopathy (aHR 8.90 [95% CI, 4.99-15.88]), and heart failure (aHR 3.63 [95% CI, 2.01-6.55]).

claims.statement: Blood pressure elevation on AAS is accompanied by measurably increased sympathetic nerve traffic, and that traffic correlates strongly with 24-hour mean BP (r=0.75). This is a mechanistic argument that the BP rise on cycle is neurally driven, not purely volume-driven — relevant because it means fluid restriction and diuretics alone are unlikely to be the answer.
claims.dose: Illicit AAS confirmed by urine chromatography-mass spectrometry
claims.population: 12 male AAS users (aged 31±2) and 9 age-matched non-users, all strength-training for at least 2 years
claims.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
claims.quote: MSNA was significantly higher in AAS users than that in AAS nonusers (29 +/- 3 vs 20 +/- 1 bursts per minute, P = 0.01)... Further analysis showed that there was a significant correlation between MSNA and 24-h mean BP (r = 0.75, P = 0.002).

claims.statement: AAS use blunts post-exercise hypotension — the normal BP drop after a training session. Controls dropped up to 13.9 mmHg systolic; AAS users managed at most 6.2 mmHg. Practically: a post-workout reading in an AAS user is not the low-water mark it would be in a non-user, and BP logs should not be anchored to post-training readings.
claims.dose: Self-administered AAS; single session of aerobic exercise with 60 min of post-exercise monitoring
claims.population: 13 AAS users (23.9±4.3 years) and 16 controls (22.1±4.5 years); small case-control study
claims.quote: While the control group had a significant reduction in post-exercise systolic blood pressure of up to 13.9±11.6mmHg at 40min, this phenomenon was limited among AAS users who reached a maximum of 6.2±11.5mmHg at 60min.

claims.statement: Left ventricular mass rose 28.3 g during a median 16-week cycle, correlated with average weekly AAS dose, and returned to baseline after a median 8 months off. Cardiac remodelling from androgens is dose-dependent and, on this timescale, reversible — which makes cycle length and dose the most powerful available levers, ahead of any antihypertensive.
claims.dose: Real-world self-selected cycles, median 16 weeks; LV mass change correlated with average weekly AAS dose
claims.population: 31 men aged 18+ intending to start an AAS cycle, 3D echocardiography before, at end of cycle, and 1 year after inclusion (HAARLEM echocardiography substudy)
claims.quote: Left ventricular mass increased with 28.3 g (CI 14.2-42.4,< 0.001) and was positively correlated with AAS average weekly dose. After a median recovery time of 8 months (T), all parameters returned to baseline.

claims.statement: Diuretics used for 'drying out' are a distinct hazard, not a blood pressure strategy: they are abused for rapid water loss and to mask other banned substances, and are prohibited by WADA both in and out of competition. This is the one antihypertensive class where the community use case and the medical use case diverge sharply.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: this source describes abuse patterns, not therapeutic dosing; diuretic choice and dose for hypertension require a prescriber monitoring electrolytes and volume status
claims.population: Athletes subject to anti-doping testing; pharmacology and toxicology review
claims.quote: Diuretics are often abused by athletes to excrete water for rapid weight loss and to mask the presence of other banned substances. Because of their abuse by athletes, diuretics have been included on The World Anti-Doping Agency's (WADA) list of prohibited substances; the use of diuretics is banned both in competition and out of competition and diuretics are routinely screened for by anti-doping laboratories.

claims.statement: Adjacent population worth naming for completeness: in transgender and gender-diverse people, the two largest studies both found testosterone associated with a rise in systolic BP, and oestrogen plus antiandrogen with a fall. The direction of effect for androgens is consistent across very different populations and dose ranges.
claims.dose: Gender-affirming hormone therapy at replacement doses; specific regimens not stated in the abstract
claims.population: Transgender and gender-diverse people on gender-affirming hormone therapy; review of prevalence and BP data
claims.quote: The two largest studies both found that estrogen plus an antiandrogen was associated with a decrease in systolic blood pressure and that testosterone was associated with an increase in systolic blood pressure.

claims.statement: In the same 11 men, crossed over, an oral 17-alpha-alkylated compound and an injectable at a supraphysiological dose produced completely different lipid outcomes. Oral stanozolol cut HDL-C by a third (HDL2 by ~three-quarters) and raised LDL-C by 29%; injectable testosterone at 200 mg/wk dropped HDL-C only 9% and LOWERED LDL-C 16%. This is the single cleanest demonstration that route, not androgenic potency, drives the lipid damage — the authors' stated hypothesis going in.
claims.dose: Stanozolol 6 mg/day orally vs testosterone enanthate 200 mg/week intramuscularly, 6 weeks each arm, crossover design
claims.population: 11 male weight lifters, healthy. Not a hypogonadal or therapeutic population; these are physique-relevant doses in trained men, which is unusually close to the app's reader.
claims.quote: We administered oral stanozolol (6 mg/d) or supraphysiological doses of intramuscular testosterone enanthate (200 mg/wk) to 11 male weight lifters for six weeks in a crossover design. Stanozolol reduced HDL-cholesterol and the HDL2 subfraction by 33% and 71%, respectively. In contrast, testosterone decreased HDL-cholesterol concentration by only 9% and the decrease was in the HDL3 subfraction. Apolipoprotein A-I level decreased 40% during stanozolol but only 8% during testosterone treatment. The low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration increased 29% with stanozolol and decreased 16% with testosterone treatment. Stanozolol, moreover, increased postheparin hepatic triglyceride lipase activity by 123%, whereas the maximum change during testosterone therapy (+25%) was not significant.

claims.statement: Direct head-to-head of an oral 17-alpha-alkylated androgen against an injectable at MATCHED weekly milligram dose (280 mg/wk of each): oral methyltestosterone dropped HDL-C 36% (1.20 to 0.77 mmol/L) while injectable testosterone enanthate produced no HDL decrease at all over 12 weeks. Only the oral arm also lost apoA-I and gained LDL-C. Critically, the HDL fall was PRECEDED by a doubling of hepatic lipase activity, and both normalised within 2 weeks of stopping the oral.
claims.dose: Total 280 mg/week for 12 weeks in each arm: methyltestosterone 20 mg orally twice daily (40 mg/day) vs testosterone enanthate 280 mg/week IM vs testosterone enanthate 280 mg/week IM + testolactone 250 mg orally four times daily
claims.population: 18 healthy lean non-smoking men aged 20-33. Eugonadal at baseline — so this measures what the drug does to a normal male lipid profile, not what replacement does to a deficient one.
claims.quote: By 4 weeks, HDL-C had decreased significantly from 1.20 +/- 0.13 to 0.77 +/- 0.13 mmol/L (MeT), from 1.18 +/- 0.15 to 0.89 +/- 0.13 mmol/L (TE TL), and demonstrated no decrease in the TE group across the time course of the study. These changes were preceded by mean increases in HTLA of 102% (MeT) and 55% (TE + TL) over baseline, and no significant change with TE. The changes in HDL-C and HTLA returned to baseline within 2 weeks of steroid cessation. There were no changes in total cholesterol, triglycerides, or insulin in any group but, in the MeT group, apo AI levels decreased and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) increased.

claims.statement: Blocking aromatisation does NOT protect lipids on androgens — it pushes them the wrong way. Adding an aromatase inhibitor to injectable testosterone made every HDL measure worse (HDL-C -16% to -20%, HDL2 -23% to -30%, apoA-I -12% to -15%) and nearly doubled the rise in hepatic lipase (+21% to +38%). The between-arm differences were not statistically significant, so this is a consistent direction rather than proof; but there is no signal here that AI use helps lipids, and a clear signal it may hurt. Paired with the Friedl finding that the non-aromatisable oral (methyltestosterone) and the AI-blocked injectable both crashed HDL while plain injectable testosterone did not, oestradiol looks protective.
claims.dose: Testosterone enanthate 200 mg/week IM, or testolactone 250 mg four times per day, or both together; randomised cross-over
claims.population: 14 male weightlifters. Testolactone is an obsolete, weak aromatase inhibitor — not anastrozole or exemestane, which is what people actually use.
claims.quote: Testosterone decreased HDL-C(-16%, P < .05), HDL2-C(-23%, NS), and apoprotein (apo) A-I (-12%, P < .05) levels, effects that were consistently but not significantly greater with simultaneous testosterone and testolactone administration (HDL-C, -20%; HDL2-C, -30%; apo A-I, -15%; P < .05 for all). In contrast, both testosterone regimens decreased HDL3-C levels by 13% (P < .05 for both). HTGLA increased 21% during testosterone treatment and 38% during combined testosterone and testolactone treatment (P < .01 for both).

claims.statement: Injectable testosterone does not move ApoB, even at 600 mg/week. Across a 5-arm dose-response from 25 to 600 mg/week for 20 weeks, apolipoprotein B, LDL-C, total cholesterol, VLDL-C and triglycerides did not change at any dose. HDL-C and apoA-I fell only in the 600 mg/wk arm, and the HDL fall was modest in absolute terms (-8 mg/dL). This is the strongest evidence that the ApoB rise seen with orals is a property of the oral 17-alpha-alkylated class, not of androgen exposure per se.
claims.dose: Testosterone enanthate 25, 50, 125, 300 or 600 mg/week IM for 20 weeks, with monthly long-acting GnRH agonist to suppress endogenous production; achieved nadir testosterone 253 to 2370 ng/dL
claims.population: 61 eugonadal men aged 18-35, randomised, dietary energy and protein standardised. Healthy young men on a controlled diet — real-world users are neither randomised nor diet-controlled, and 20 weeks is short.
claims.quote: Plasma high density lipoprotein cholesterol and apolipoprotein A-I concentrations were inversely correlated with total and free T concentrations and were significantly decreased only in the 600 mg/wk group (change in high density lipoprotein cholesterol: -8 +/- 2 mg/dl; P = 0.0005; change in apolipoprotein A-I: -16 +/- 2 mg/dl; P = 0.0001). Serum total cholesterol, low density lipoprotein cholesterol, very low density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoprotein B, and apolipoprotein C-III were not significantly correlated with T dose or concentration.
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism

claims.statement: Real-world self-administered stacks: ApoB rose 38% (0.96 to 1.32 g/L) while HDL-C fell 60% (1.08 to 0.43 mmol/L), HDL2 fell 76%, and apoA-I fell 50%. Total cholesterol and triglycerides did not change significantly — meaning a standard lipid panel showing 'normal cholesterol' can completely mask this. Lp(a) fell sharply (189 to 32 U/L), which is the one favourable move and is often cited by users as offsetting; the authors do not accept that framing.
claims.dose: Self-administered AAS regimens for 8 or 14 weeks; the abstract does not state which compounds, routes or doses were used, so this magnitude cannot be attributed to orals specifically
claims.population: 19 healthy male strength athletes self-administering AAS, compared with 16 non-using volunteers; non-blinded observational arm of a two-part study
claims.quote: In study 1 AAS administration led to decreases in serum concentrations of HDL-C (from 1.08 (0.30) to 0.43 (0.22) mmol/l), HDL2-C (from 0.21 (0.18) to 0.05 (0.03) mmol/l), HDL3-C (from 0.87 (0.24) to 0.40 (0.20) mmol/l, and Apo-A1 (from 1.41 (0.27) to 0.71 (0.34) g/l), whereas Apo-B increased from 0.96 (0.13) to 1.32 (0.28) g/l. Serum Lp(a) declined from 189 (315) to 32 (63) U/l.

claims.statement: In the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled arm of the same paper, a pure injectable — nandrolone decanoate 200 mg/week for 8 weeks — moved NOTHING: not triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL-C, HDL2, HDL3, apoA-I or ApoB. The only change was a selective Lp(a) reduction. This is the internal control that makes the study-1 numbers interpretable: the catastrophic lipid profile came from the stacks, not from injectable anabolic exposure as such.
claims.dose: Nandrolone decanoate 200 mg/week intramuscularly for 8 weeks, randomised double-blind vs placebo
claims.population: 16 bodybuilders. Small (n=16), short (8 weeks), and not powered for ApoB — a null here is not proof of lipid neutrality at longer durations or higher doses.
claims.quote: In study 2, nandrolone decanoate did not influence serum triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL-C, HDL2-C, HDL3-C, Apo-A1, and Apo-B concentrations after four and eight weeks of intervention, nor six weeks after withdrawal. However, Lp(a) concentrations decreased significantly from 103 (68) to 65 (44) U/l in the nandrolone decanoate group, and in the placebo group a smaller reduction from 245 (245) to 201 (194) U/l was observed.

claims.statement: Stopping does not produce a fast fix after real-world stacks: six weeks after cessation, HDL-C, HDL2, apoA-I, ApoB and Lp(a) had all still not returned to baseline, and recovery was slower after 14 weeks of use than after 8. Practical implication: a lipid panel drawn shortly after a cycle ends is still a drug-affected panel, and 'off-cycle' bloodwork timed at 4-6 weeks will understate the recovery time. Note this conflicts with Friedl, where methyltestosterone monotherapy normalised HDL and hepatic lipase within 2 weeks — duration and polypharmacy appear to determine how long the damage persists.
claims.dose: Self-administered AAS for 8 or 14 weeks, then cessation; compounds and doses not specified in the abstract
claims.population: 19 healthy male strength athletes self-administering AAS, followed 6 weeks after withdrawal
claims.quote: Six weeks after AAS cessation, serum HDL-C, HDL2-C, Apo-A1, Apo-B, and Lp(a) had still not returned to baseline concentrations. Administration of AAS for 14 weeks was associated with slower recovery to pretreatment concentrations than administration for eight weeks.

claims.statement: The mechanism is hepatic lipase induction — but not only that. Two weeks of oral stanozolol raised hepatic lipase activity 277% in normal controls, with HDL-C down 49%, HDL2 down 90% and apoA-I down 41%. In a man genetically unable to make hepatic lipase, stanozolol still cut HDL-C 20%, HDL2 48% and apoA-I 32%. So a second, hepatic-lipase-independent pathway exists — which matters because it means anything aimed only at the lipase pathway cannot fully undo the effect.
claims.dose: Stanozolol 6 mg/day orally for 2 weeks
claims.population: Two brothers with hepatic triglyceride lipase deficiency (both with coronary heart disease) plus two controls — n=4 total. Extremely small, and the controls were older men, not young athletes. Direction is robust across the literature; the exact percentages are not.
claims.quote: Consistent with other reports, HL activity increased a mean of 277% in controls with a concomitant decrease in HDL cholesterol (49%), HDL2 cholesterol (90%), HDL3 cholesterol (16%), and apo A-I (41%) and no change in apo A-II. Although stanozolol failed to induce HL activity in the HL-deficient man, HDL cholesterol, HDL2 cholesterol, and apo A-I were reduced a mean of 20%, 48%, and 32%, respectively.

claims.statement: Oxandrolone is not the benign oral. At just 4 mg/day for 28 days it drove HDL-C below 40 mg/dL in 7 of 10 type IV and 3 of 6 type IIb patients, and raised LDL-C in 8 of 10 type IV patients — while lowering triglycerides and VLDL ApoB. The ApoB was redistributed out of VLDL and into LDL, which is exactly the shift that a triglyceride-focused reading of a lipid panel would misread as an improvement.
claims.dose: Oxandrolone 4 mg/day orally for 28 days
claims.population: Adults with type IIa, IIb and IV hyperlipoproteinaemia (n roughly 20 across types). A dyslipidaemic patient population, not healthy athletes, and 4 mg/day is far below physique-use oxandrolone doses.
claims.doi: none assigned — no DOI in PubMed or Europe PMC; use https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/231951/
claims.quote: Oxandrolone (4 mg/day, for 28 days) induced a significant reduction in plasma and VLDL triglyceride. Reciprocal elevation of LDL cholesterol was observed in 8 of 10 type IV patients and in 2 of 5 type IIb patients. In patients with type IV hyperlipoproteinemia, significant reduction of plasma apolipoproteinB and VLDL apolipoprotein B and inverse LDL apolipoprotein B increment was observed after treatment with oxandrolone. HDL cholesterol was decreased. Hypo-high density lipoproteinemia defined as HDL cholesterol concentration below 40 mg/100 ml occurred in 7 of 10 type IV, 3 of 6 type IIb and 1 of 4 type IIa patients.

claims.statement: There is no oral dose low enough to spare HDL. A 2-year randomised placebo-controlled trial of oxandrolone at 0.06 mg/kg/day — roughly 4-5 mg/day in a 70 kg adult, a genuinely microdose regimen — still lowered HDL cholesterol at P < 0.001, alongside a favourable triglyceride drop. This directly undercuts the common harm-reduction assumption that a low oral dose avoids the lipid penalty.
claims.dose: Oral oxandrolone 0.06 mg/kg/day (or placebo) for 2 years
claims.population: 93 prepubertal boys with Klinefelter syndrome, aged 4-12, randomised and double-blind. Children on a 2-year continuous low dose — very different pharmacology and body size from an adult on a 6-8 week cycle, so treat the direction as transferable and the magnitude as not.
claims.quote: Ox resulted in lower triglycerides (P = 0.043), but also lower high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (P < 0.001) and a more rapid advancement in bone age (P = 0.011).
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism

claims.statement: Switching from the oral to an injectable reverses the lipid damage — demonstrated inside a single trial, unplanned. The oral oxandrolone arm developed a significant HDL-C fall and LDL-C rise severe enough that the investigators stopped it at 3 months and moved those men to injectable nandrolone decanoate; the injectable then reversed the lipoprotein changes. This is the only prospective within-subject evidence retrieved that route-switching, rather than stopping entirely, restores the lipid profile.
claims.dose: Oral oxandrolone for 3 months (dose not stated in the abstract), then switched to parenteral nandrolone decanoate injections given every 2 weeks (dose not stated in the abstract) for months 3-9
claims.population: 30 healthy obese men aged 40-60 with low-normal serum testosterone (2-5 ng/mL), all undergoing dietary weight loss. Confounded by concurrent weight loss, and the abstract states neither drug's dose — so no dosing number can be taken from this study.
claims.doi: none assigned — no DOI in PubMed or Europe PMC; use https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8574271/
claims.quote: There was a significant decrease in HDL-C, and increase in LDL-C in the ASOX group, which led to their being switched to the parenteral nandrolone decanoate (ASND) after 3 months. [...] ASND reversed the effects of ASOX on lipoproteins and thyroid hormones.
claims.journal: International Journal of Obesity and Related Metabolic Disorders

claims.statement: Long-term oral danazol raises ApoB-100 and LDL and lowers HDL and apoA-I versus two separate control groups — and total cholesterol and triglycerides were NOT different. This is the clearest demonstration in the retrieved set that on an oral androgen, standard cholesterol and triglyceride numbers can look unremarkable while the atherogenic particle count is measurably up. If only one extra test is run on an oral, ApoB is the one that carries information a lipid panel does not.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the abstract does not state the danazol doses used for long-term HAE prophylaxis. The FDA label dose for hereditary angioedema is 200 mg two or three times a day, then individually titrated to the lowest effective dose.
claims.population: Patients with hereditary angioedema on long-term danazol prophylaxis, compared with HAE patients not on prophylaxis and with untreated healthy subjects. This is on-label therapeutic danazol in a patient population, not physique dosing.
claims.quote: Serum concentrations of HDL ( P = .0002 and P < .0001) and apolipoprotein A-I ( P = .0015 and P < .0001) were significantly lower, whereas LDL ( P = .0129 and P = .0127) and apolipoprotein B-100 ( P = .0456 and P = .0013) were higher in the danazol-treated patients compared with the 2 control groups, respectively. No significant difference was found in total cholesterol, triglyceride, or lipoprotein(a) levels.
claims.journal: The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology

claims.statement: Pooled across 19 studies and 272 hypogonadal men, injectable testosterone esters at replacement dosing moved HDL-C down only 4 mg/dL — and moved total cholesterol down 14 mg/dL and LDL-C down 5 mg/dL at the same time. In other words, at replacement dose by injection, the net lipid picture is neutral-to-slightly-favourable, which is a different world from the oral 17-alpha-alkylated numbers. Counterintuitively, the HDL decrease was LARGER at lower testosterone doses.
claims.dose: Meta-analytic average: 179 +/- 13 mg intramuscular testosterone ester every 16 +/- 1 days for 6 +/- 1 months
claims.population: 272 hypogonadal men, mean age 44, mean baseline total testosterone 0.5 ng/mL; 20% hypergonadotropic. Genuinely hypogonadal men being brought to normal — not eugonadal men being pushed above normal.
claims.quote: Fixed-effects estimates of post-treatment minus pretreatment differences were -14 [-17 to -11] mg/dL (total cholesterol), -5 [-8 to -1] mg/dL (LDL cholesterol), -4 [-5 to -2] mg/dL (HDL cholesterol), and -1 [-6 to + 4] mg/dL (triglyceride).

claims.statement: The important counterexample to 'injectables are safe for lipids': in severely hypogonadal men starting from a washed-out baseline, EVERY route — oral testosterone undecanoate, oral mesterolone, IM enanthate and a subcutaneous implant — raised LDL-C by 34-65% and dropped HDL-C by 31-36%, with no correlation to achieved testosterone level. The authors read this as androgen exposure moving a female-pattern lipid profile to a male-pattern one, with the threshold far below the normal male range. Read this as: the direction of change depends heavily on where you started, and injectables are not lipid-free.
claims.dose: Mesterolone 100 mg orally daily; testosterone undecanoate 160 mg orally daily; testosterone enanthate 250 mg IM every 21 days; single subcutaneous implant of crystalline testosterone 1,200 mg. All for 189 days.
claims.population: 55 hypogonadal men randomised, all with baseline serum testosterone <3.6 nmol/L after >=3 months androgen washout, and all with normal baseline cholesterol and triglycerides. The extreme baseline (mean T <3 nmol/L) is the whole reason the percentage changes are so large — these numbers do not transfer to someone starting from a normal or supraphysiological level.
claims.quote: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) also increased significantly by 34.3% +/- 5.5% (TU), 46.4% +/- 4.1% (MES), 65.2% +/- 5.7% (TE), and 47.5% +/- 4.3% (TPEL). High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) showed a significant decrease by -30.9% +/- 2.8% (TU), -34.9% +/- 2.5% (MES), -35.7% +/- 2.6% (TE), and -32.5% +/- 3.5% (TPEL). Serum TG significantly increased by 37.3% +/- 11.3% (TU), 46.4% +/- 10.3% (MES), 29.4% +/- 6.5% (TE), and 22.9% +/- 6.7% (TPEL).

claims.statement: The HDL number understates the problem: in AAS users the remaining HDL also works less well. Cholesterol efflux capacity was significantly lower in users than in matched strength-trained non-users (20% vs 23% vs 24%), and efflux fell further the longer someone had used. In the same cohort, 25% of users had plaque in at least two coronary arteries and NONE of the non-users or sedentary controls had any. So restoring the HDL-C number alone is not evidence that HDL function has been restored.
claims.dose: Not applicable — cross-sectional observation of self-selected use; compounds and doses not standardised
claims.population: 20 strength-trained male AAS users aged 29 +/- 5, 20 age-matched strength-trained non-users, 10 sedentary controls. Cross-sectional, so causation is inferred not proven, and n=20 per group is small for a plaque prevalence estimate.
claims.quote: Cholesterol efflux was lower in AASU compared with AASNU and SC (20 vs. 23 vs. 24%, respectively, p < 0.001). However, the lag time for LDL oxidation was higher in AASU compared with AASNU and SC (41 vs 13 vs 11 min, respectively, p < 0.001). We found at least 2 coronary arteries with plaques in 25% of AASU. None of the AASNU and SC had plaques. The time of AAS use was negatively associated with cholesterol efflux.

claims.statement: The lipid changes track a hard imaging endpoint, and the relationship is cumulative-dose dependent. In 140 weightlifters, AAS users had higher coronary plaque volume than non-users, and each additional 10 years of cumulative AAS use predicted a 0.60 SD increase in plaque volume rank. Users also had reduced LV systolic and diastolic function, worse in those currently on-drug than those currently off — meaning some of the cardiac effect is reversible and the atherosclerosis is not.
claims.dose: Cumulative lifetime exposure, self-reported; >=2 years of cumulative lifetime AAS use to qualify as a user. Individual compounds, routes and doses not standardised.
claims.population: 140 experienced male weightlifters aged 34-54: 86 with >=2 years cumulative lifetime AAS use, 54 non-users. Cross-sectional cohort with self-reported exposure — recall bias and selection into use are unaddressed.
claims.quote: In addition, AAS users demonstrated higher coronary artery plaque volume than nonusers (median [interquartile range] 3 [0, 174] mLversus 0 [0, 69] mL;=0.012). Lifetime AAS dose was strongly associated with coronary atherosclerotic burden (increase [95% confidence interval] in rank of plaque volume for each 10-year increase in cumulative duration of AAS use: 0.60 SD units [0.16-1.03 SD units];=0.008).

claims.statement: Replicated in 2025, in both sexes, at much shorter median exposure. In 164 Danish recreational athletes with a median cumulative lifetime AAS use of only 2.2 years, longer cumulative use predicted higher odds of a positive coronary calcium score (OR 1.23 per unit) and of non-calcified coronary plaque (OR 1.17), and exposure beyond 5 years was associated with more severe calcification. Roughly a quarter of the active users were women — the only retrieved cardiovascular-imaging evidence that includes female users.
claims.dose: Cumulative lifetime AAS use; median 2.2 years (IQR 1.2-7.2) in active users. Compounds and doses not standardised; use was biochemically confirmed.
claims.population: 164 recreational athletes aged 18+ recruited from fitness centres in Denmark: 80 active users (median age 35, 61 men / 19 women), 26 previous users, 58 non-users. Cross-sectional; unadjusted group differences in plaque and CAC were mostly non-significant and the dose-response only appeared after confounder adjustment.
claims.quote: However, in confounder-adjusted logistic regression, longer cumulative lifetime AAS use was associated with higher odds of a positive CAC score (OR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.09-1.39; P = .001) and presence of coronary NCPs (OR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.05-1.30; P = .004). AAS use exceeding 5 years was associated with greater severity of calcifications (n = 94; χ2 = 9.78; P = .04).

claims.statement: Training does not protect you. Bodybuilders started with a far better lipid profile than powerlifters (HDL-C 55 vs 38 mg/dL, LDL/HDL ratio 2.0 vs 3.7) purely from training style — and androgen use then dropped HDL-C and HDL2 by 55% and raised LDL-C by 61% in both groups alike, sending the LDL/HDL ratio up 280%. High-volume training buys a better baseline; it does not blunt the drug effect on top of it.
claims.dose: Self-administered androgens; compounds and doses not specified. Subjects were studied before and after their own androgen use.
claims.population: 8 bodybuilders and 4 powerlifters studied before and after androgen use, with 8 age- and body-fat-matched runners as an additional comparison. Very small (n=12 on drug), self-selected, and 1984-era compounds — but the before/after within-subject design is what gives it weight.
claims.quote: Androgen use by eight bodybuilders and four powerlifters lowered values of both HDL-C and HDL2-C by 55% and raised values of LDL-C (61% +/- 10%) and LDL-C/HDL-C ratios (280% +/- 40%).

claims.statement: A caution on the most obvious mitigation: statins and oral androgens can interact dangerously. Coadministration of danazol 600 mg/day with lovastatin 40 mg/day was associated with rhabdomyolysis (CK 68,193 U/L) and pancreatitis, resolving on withdrawal of both. This is a single case with heavy confounding (end-stage renal disease, an explicitly excessive lovastatin dose), so it is a signal to have a prescriber pick the statin and the dose — not evidence that statins are contraindicated on androgens.
claims.dose: Danazol 600 mg/day plus lovastatin 40 mg/day (the report itself notes the lovastatin dose was 'a particularly high dose and not recommended')
claims.population: One 59-year-old Asian woman with end-stage renal disease, hypertension and diabetes, receiving danazol for thrombocytopenia. n=1, multiple confounders, and ESRD independently raises rhabdomyolysis risk.
claims.quote: Her medical records also revealed that lovastatin 40 mg/d (a particularly high dose and not recommended) had been administered for 7 weeks, and danazol 600 mg/d was added ( approximately 15 days later) to treat thrombocytopenia due to hypoplastic bone marrow. Laboratory findings revealed elevated creatine kinase (68,193 U/L), elevated pancreatic enzymes (amylase/lipase, 361/2788 U/L), and elevated liver enzymes (aspartate/alanine aminotransferase, 1496/1493 U/L), consistent with rhabdomyolysis and pancreatitis.

claims.statement: In the largest long-term cohort of testosterone-treated trans men (n=1073, 20-year follow-up), erythrocytosis by threshold was 11% above hematocrit 0.50, 3.7% above 0.52, and 0.5% above 0.54. The steepest rise is in year 1 (0.39 to 0.45 L/L), but cumulative risk keeps climbing: 10% at one year, 38% at ten years. Monitoring cannot stop after year 1.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: this cohort study reports no doses or formulations in the abstract, only administration route as a risk factor
claims.population: 1073 adult trans men on gender-affirming testosterone at a single Amsterdam gender clinic, monitored up to 20 years. Testosterone is not FDA-approved for gender-affirming care, so these are off-label users — but they are prescriber-monitored, unlike self-managed users.
claims.quote: Erythrocytosis occurred in 11% (hematocrit > 0.50 L/L), 3.7% (hematocrit > 0.52 L/L), and 0.5% (hematocrit > 0.54 L/L) of trans men. ... In the first year of testosterone therapy hematocrit increased most: 0.39 L/L at baseline to 0.45 L/L after 1 year. Although there was only a slight continuation of this increase in the following 20 years, the probability of developing erythrocytosis still increased (10% after 1 year, 38% after 10 years).
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism

claims.statement: Modifiable and non-modifiable predictors of crossing hematocrit 0.50 on testosterone, with effect sizes: smoking (OR 2.2), long-acting undecanoate injections (OR 2.9), older age at initiation (OR 5.9), higher BMI (OR 3.7), and pre-existing pulmonary conditions (OR 2.5). The authors' first-line response is behavioural and route-based, not phlebotomy.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the recommended first step is a route change (to transdermal) plus smoking cessation and weight loss, with no dose figure given
claims.population: Same 1073 trans men. The risk factors (smoking, BMI, sleep-disordered breathing) are shared with cis men on TRT and with self-managing users, so the direction of effect likely transfers even though the absolute rates may not.
claims.quote: Tobacco use (odds ratio [OR] 2.2; 95% CI, 1.6-3.3), long-acting undecanoate injections (OR 2.9; 95% CI, 1.7-5.0), age at initiation of hormone therapy (OR 5.9; 95% CI, 2.8-12.3), body mass index (BMI) (OR 3.7; 95% CI, 2.2-6.2), and pulmonary conditions associated with erythrocytosis and polycythemia vera (OR 2.5; 95% CI, 1.4-4.4) were associated with hematocrit > 0.50 L/L. ... A reasonable first step in the care for trans men with erythrocytosis while on testosterone is to advise them to quit smoking, to switch to a transdermal administration route, and if BMI is high, to lose weight.
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism

claims.statement: At a median 100 mg weekly of injectable testosterone cypionate, severe erythrocytosis is rare: over 20 months, cumulative incidence was 12.6% for hematocrit >50.4%, 1.0% for >52%, and 0.6% for >54%. This is the cleanest dose-anchored incidence figure available for weekly IM cypionate.
claims.dose: 100 mg weekly (median) injectable testosterone cypionate
claims.population: 282 people receiving gender-affirming testosterone, first 20 months of therapy. All were on injectable cypionate. Absolute rates in older cis men with higher baseline hematocrit will be higher than this.
claims.quote: During the first 20 months of testosterone therapy, the cumulative incidence of hematocrit >50.4% was 12.6%, hematocrit >52% was 1.0%, and hematocrit >54% was 0.6%. All people were taking injectable testosterone cypionate, with a median dose of 100 mg weekly.

claims.statement: In 6670 people on gender-affirming testosterone, 8.4% had hematocrit >=50%, 2.7% >=52%, and 0.9% >=54%. Route matters and is measurable: intramuscular users averaged 44.96% vs 43.41% transdermal, with both route and serum testosterone level independently associated with hematocrit.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: doses not reported; the comparison is by route (intramuscular vs transdermal) and by serum testosterone band (<50, 50-299, 300-999, >=1000 ng/dL)
claims.population: 6670 patients prescribed testosterone through a national US telehealth gender-affirming care provider — a real-world, largely unselected population, but cross-sectional (single paired lab values), so it undercounts anyone whose peak was missed.
claims.quote: Among 6670 individuals, 560 (8.4%) had a hematocrit ≥50%, 182 ≥ 52% (2.7%), and 60 ≥ 54% (0.9%). ... Patients on intramuscular testosterone had a higher mean hematocrit than those on transdermal testosterone (44.96% vs 43.41%, P < .001). Both route of administration (P < .001) and testosterone level (P < .001) had statistically significant associations with hematocrit when controlling for each other.
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism

claims.statement: Erythropoiesis is linearly dose-dependent on testosterone, and older men respond more strongly to the same dose. This is the randomized dose-response evidence behind 'lower the dose' as an intervention.
claims.dose: Testosterone enanthate 25, 50, 125, 300, or 600 mg IM weekly for 20 weeks (with monthly GnRH agonist to suppress endogenous production)
claims.population: 60 older men aged 60-75 and 61 young men aged 19-35, healthy, in a controlled dose-response study. Endogenous testosterone was clamped off, so these are clean exogenous dose effects — closer to a self-managing user's physiology than a partial-replacement TRT study.
claims.quote: Hemoglobin and hematocrit increased significantly in a linear, dose-dependent fashion in both young and older men in response to graded doses of testosterone (P<0.0001). The increases in hemoglobin and hematocrit were significantly greater in older than young men.
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism

claims.statement: Mechanism, and why iron is entangled with this: testosterone raises erythropoietin and suppresses hepcidin, driving iron out of stores and into red cells, then resets the EPO/hemoglobin set point so the higher hematocrit is defended rather than transient. Ferritin falls as a direct pharmacological effect of testosterone, before any phlebotomy.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: 'testosterone gel daily for 6 months' — the abstract gives no milligram dose
claims.population: Older men with mobility limitation, randomized to testosterone gel or placebo for 6 months. The 7-10% hemoglobin/hematocrit rise is a replacement-dose effect; the set-point mechanism means a hematocrit lowered by phlebotomy will be actively pushed back up while testosterone continues.
claims.quote: The 7%-10% increase in hemoglobin and hematocrit, respectively, with testosterone administration was associated with significantly increased erythropoietin (EPO) levels and decreased ferritin and hepcidin levels at 1 and 3 months. At 6 months, EPO and hepcidin levels returned toward baseline in spite of continued testosterone administration, but EPO levels remained nonsuppressed even though elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit higher than at baseline, suggesting a new set point.
claims.journal: The Journals of Gerontology Series A

claims.statement: In 347 men on injectable testosterone undecanoate followed prospectively, 7% exceeded hematocrit 0.50, 4% exceeded 0.52 and 1% exceeded 0.54 — and the specialist andrology unit's stated management was lengthening the injection interval, not phlebotomy.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: management was 'optimising inter-injection interval' for testosterone undecanoate; the abstract specifies no interval in weeks
claims.population: 347 patients receiving 3022 testosterone undecanoate injections over 3.5 years at a hospital andrology clinic in Sydney. Long-acting undecanoate; findings do not transfer directly to weekly short-ester injecting.
claims.quote: Mean haematocrit was 0.44±0.04 (s.d.) with 25 (7%) >0.50, 14 (4%) >0.52 and 3 (1%) >0.54. ... polycythaemia was a minor problem rarely requiring treatment other than optimising inter-injection interval.

claims.statement: At an identical 100 mg weekly dose, subcutaneous testosterone enanthate produced significantly lower hematocrit than intramuscular testosterone cypionate. The peak-to-trough profile, not just the weekly milligram total, drives erythrocytosis.
claims.dose: 100 mg weekly, IM testosterone cypionate vs 100 mg weekly subcutaneous testosterone enanthate autoinjector; outcomes at 12 weeks
claims.population: 234 hypogonadal men in urology practice. Non-randomized comparison with regression adjustment, 12-week horizon only — it does not tell you whether the difference persists at a year.
claims.quote: A total of 234 hypogonadal men were treated with testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) via IM-TC 100 mg weekly or SCTE-AI 100 mg weekly. ... SCTE-AI was independently associated with lower post-therapy E2 (p <0.001) and HCT (p <0.001).

claims.statement: The honest starting point on thresholds: no hematocrit threshold has ever been tested prospectively in testosterone users. The largest attempt to attach a number to risk found that developing hematocrit >=52% on testosterone was associated with more MACE/VTE in year one — 5.15% vs 3.87%, OR 1.35 — while testosterone itself, in men who did not develop polycythemia, showed no excess risk versus untreated hypogonadal men.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: a database study with no dose or formulation data; polycythemia defined as hematocrit >=52%
claims.population: 5842 matched pairs of men with total testosterone <350 ng/dL receiving testosterone therapy, drawn from a 74-million-patient claims/EHR database. Propensity-matched but not randomized: men who develop erythrocytosis differ from those who do not (BMI, smoking, sleep apnea, adherence), and residual confounding could produce an OR of this size on its own.
claims.quote: An unsafe hematocrit threshold for men receiving testosterone therapy (TT) has never been tested. ... Men with polycythemia had a higher risk of MACE/VTE (number of outcomes: 301, 5.15%) than men who had normal hematocrit (226, 3.87%) while on TT (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.13-1.61, p <0.001). In hypogonadal men who received testosterone, no increased risk of MACE and VTE was identified as compared to hypogonadal men naïve to TT.

claims.statement: The counterweight: in 519 people on gender-affirming testosterone, 20% crossed hematocrit 50% but thromboembolic events occurred in only 0.9%, and most events were minor (superficial and calf vein thrombosis). This study also documents what clinicians actually do — 42% of those with erythrocytosis had a dose reduction, only 4.8% underwent phlebotomy.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: doses not reported; the actionable figure is that dose reduction was the intervention in 42% of erythrocytosis cases and phlebotomy in 4.8%
claims.population: 923 transgender and non-binary adults on testosterone (519 with paired pre/post labs) at a US academic centre, plus a national inpatient sample. Young population with low baseline cardiovascular risk — event rates would be higher in older men with vascular disease.
claims.quote: Mean time-to-peak Hgb/Hct was 31.2 months; 7.8% developed a hemoglobin >17.5 g/dL, whereas 20% developed a hematocrit of >50%. Testosterone dose reduction occurred in 42% of patients with erythrocytosis and 4.8% underwent phlebotomy. Thromboembolic events occurred in 0.9%, of which 80% had developed erythrocytosis by either Hgb or Hct ... Despite the high incidence of erythrocytosis, thromboembolic events and hospitalizations involving erythrocytosis were uncommon.

claims.statement: In 1.5 million blood donors, high hemoglobin tracked arterial events (men >=17.5 g/dL: HR 3.52 for MI, 2.36 for ischemic stroke) but NOT venous ones — venous thrombosis risk was highest in men with LOW hemoglobin (<13.0 g/dL, HR 1.69). And when each person was compared only to himself, the MI association weakened. The authors call high hemoglobin a risk marker, not a demonstrated cause.
claims.dose: none — an observational cohort with no intervention; the parameters are hemoglobin bands, not drug doses
claims.population: 1,538,019 Swedish and Danish blood donors, 1987-2012. Blood donors are healthier than average and this is not a testosterone population — but it is the largest dataset on whether a hemoglobin number predicts clots in people without polycythemia vera, and it argues against treating high hematocrit as a VTE predictor.
claims.quote: The HRs for myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke in men with hemoglobin concentration ≥ 17.5 g/dL were 3.52 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.85-4.36) and 2.36 (95% CI, 1.63-3.43), respectively, compared to the reference group. ... The risk of venous thrombosis was highest in men with subnormal hemoglobin concentration (<13.0 g/dL), HR 1.69 (95% CI, 1.40-2.04). In the person-stratified model, the association between elevated hemoglobin concentration and risk of myocardial infarction was attenuated but remained significant.

claims.statement: The only randomized trial ever to test a hematocrit target found a target of <45% beat 45-50% (2.7% vs 9.8% cardiovascular death or major thrombosis, HR 3.91) — but it was done in JAK2-positive polycythemia vera, a clonal blood cancer with abnormal platelets and white cells. This trial is the origin of the intuition that 'lower hematocrit is safer', and it does not transfer to drug-induced secondary erythrocytosis.
claims.dose: Hematocrit target <45% vs 45-50%, achieved with phlebotomy, hydroxyurea, or both; median follow-up 31 months
claims.population: 365 adults with JAK2-positive polycythemia vera. NOT testosterone users. Nothing about this population — clonal marrow disease, abnormal platelet function, older age — makes its result portable to someone whose hematocrit rose because of an injected androgen.
claims.quote: Current treatment recommendations for patients with polycythemia vera call for maintaining a hematocrit of less than 45%, but this therapeutic strategy has not been tested in a randomized clinical trial. We randomly assigned 365 adults with JAK2-positive polycythemia vera ... the primary end point was recorded in 5 of 182 patients in the low-hematocrit group (2.7%) and 18 of 183 patients in the high-hematocrit group (9.8%) (hazard ratio in the high-hematocrit group, 3.91; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.45 to 10.53; P=0.007).
claims.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine

claims.statement: Haematologists who specialise in erythrocytosis explicitly advise against routine phlebotomy for non-clonal (non-polycythemia-vera) erythrocytosis, including drug-induced erythrocytosis from testosterone. If phlebotomy is used at all, they say frequency should be driven by symptoms, not by the hematocrit number.
claims.dose: Therapeutic phlebotomy 'with frequency determined by symptoms rather than Hct level'; plus cardiovascular risk optimization and low-dose aspirin — no volume or interval specified
claims.population: Expert review covering the full differential of JAK2-unmutated erythrocytosis, with testosterone named as a drug cause alongside erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and SGLT2 inhibitors. This is expert opinion, graded by the authors themselves as not supported by hard evidence.
claims.quote: Current consensus treatment guidelines are not supported by hard evidence and their value is further undermined by limited phenotypic characterization and unfounded concerns for thrombosis. We are of the opinion that cytoreductive therapy and indiscriminate use of phlebotomy should be avoided in the treatment of non-clonal erythrocytosis. However, it is reasonable to consider therapeutic phlebotomy if one were to demonstrate value in symptom control, with frequency determined by symptoms rather than Hct level.

claims.statement: There is no evidence that therapeutic phlebotomy is either effective or safe for testosterone-induced erythrocytosis, and a plausible mechanism by which it makes things worse: it lowers tissue oxygen tension and depletes iron stores, both of which can drive erythropoiesis harder and may raise thrombotic risk. The authors call for shared decision-making rather than reflex phlebotomy.
claims.dose: none — the paper's point is that no effective or safe phlebotomy regimen has been established for this indication
claims.population: Narrative review by a group that runs a clinic for people using performance and image-enhancing drugs, so the framing is closer to the self-managing user than most TRT literature. It is a review, not new data — it establishes an evidence gap, not an effect.
claims.quote: However, evidence supporting the efficacy or safety of therapeutic phlebotomy in lowering hematocrit in TTh-induced erythrocytosis is lacking. In light of this dearth of evidence, the recommendation to lower hematocrit using therapeutic phlebotomy is notable, as phlebotomy lowers tissue oxygen partial pressure (pO2) and eventually depletes iron stores, thereby triggering various biological pathways which might increase thrombotic risk.

claims.statement: A 2025 endocrine review states the management hierarchy explicitly: re-evaluate whether testosterone is indicated at all, fix modifiable risk factors, switch to transdermal, and/or cut the dose — and does not recommend venesection except for clonal erythrocytosis, citing its potential pro-thrombotic effects.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the interventions are ranked (indication review, risk-factor modification, transdermal switch, dose reduction) without numeric targets; venesection is explicitly not recommended outside clonal disease
claims.population: Review addressed to clinicians treating men with functional hypogonadism, obesity, hypertension or type 2 diabetes — the group most likely to be co-prescribed SGLT2 inhibitors, which independently raise hematocrit. Review-level evidence, not a trial.
claims.quote: Management strategies include re-evaluating the original treatment indication, addressing modifiable risk factors, switching to transdermal testosterone and/or reducing the testosterone dose. Venesection is not recommended, except for clonal erythrocytosis, due to its potential pro-thrombotic effects.

claims.statement: Blood donation does not work as a substitute for managing erythrocytosis. Among men on testosterone presenting as blood donors, hemoglobin was >=180 g/L (calculated hematocrit >=54%) at 25% of appointments, and 44% of repeat donors were still above that threshold at subsequent donations. The authors specifically warn about the misperception that donating has removed the risk.
claims.dose: Standard whole-blood donation at volunteer-donor intervals; the finding is that this schedule was insufficient to hold hematocrit below 54%
claims.population: 39 men on testosterone replacement identified among blood donors in Southwestern Ontario over 2 years, 108 clinic visits. Small, and donors self-identified — but it is the only direct measurement of whether donation actually controls hematocrit in this group.
claims.quote: Hemoglobin concentrations of 180 g/L or more (calculated hematocrit, ≥54%) were measured at 25% of appointments. Of the 27 repeat donors, 12 (44%) had persistently elevated hemoglobin levels (≥180 g/L) at subsequent donations. ... These data also suggest that repeat blood donation was insufficient to maintain a hematocrit below 54%. Our findings raise concerns about the persistent risk of vascular events in these donors, particularly when coupled with the misperception by patients and health care providers that donation has reduced or eliminated the risks of TRT-induced polycythemia.

claims.statement: The iron cost of repeated blood removal, quantified in a randomized trial: after a single 500 mL whole-blood donation, 67% of people who took no iron had still not recovered their iron stores at 168 days. With 37.5 mg elemental iron daily, hemoglobin recovery took about 31-32 days instead of 78-158 days. One donation every 8 weeks without iron is a net drain.
claims.dose: Ferrous gluconate 37.5 mg elemental iron, one tablet daily for 24 weeks (168 days) after a 500 mL whole-blood donation
claims.population: 215 US blood donors aged 18-79 who had not donated in 4 months, stratified by ferritin (<=26 vs >26 ng/mL). NOT people phlebotomized for testosterone erythrocytosis — who are typically bled more often than every 8 weeks, and whose hepcidin is suppressed by testosterone, so their iron kinetics are not identical.
claims.quote: Compared with participants who did not receive iron supplementation, those who received iron supplementation had shortened time to 80% hemoglobin recovery in both the low-ferritin (mean, 32 days, interquartile range [IQR], 30-34, vs 158 days, IQR, 126->168) and higher-ferritin groups (31 days, IQR, 29-33, vs 78 days, IQR, 66-95). ... Without iron supplements, 67% of participants did not recover iron stores by 168 days.

claims.statement: Iron repletion after phlebotomy has randomized dosing evidence in donors: 60 mg elemental iron daily was the most effective arm, reducing iron deficiency at 56 days to 1% versus 51% on placebo; 30 mg daily and alternate-day schedules were also effective. Alternate-day dosing performed nearly as well as daily.
claims.dose: Ferrous bisglycinate 30 mg or 60 mg elemental iron, daily or alternate days, for 56 days (compared with placebo)
claims.population: 830 whole-blood donors with ferritin <=30 ug/L in the Netherlands. Again donors, not people bled for testosterone erythrocytosis — and note the tension: replacing iron in someone whose hematocrit is being deliberately held down will also refuel erythropoiesis. That trade-off has not been studied.
claims.quote: At 56 days, 55 (51%) of 108 participants in the placebo daily group ... and four (4%) of 110 participants in the 60 mg alternate day group presented with iron deficiency. ... In regular donors with low ferritin, iron supplementation-60 mg taken daily, in particular-effectively mitigates iron deficiency, low ferritin, and low haemoglobin.

claims.statement: A 2024 American Society of Hematology education review states plainly that thrombotic risk on gender-affirming testosterone appears low, that polycythemia is the common problem requiring monitoring and hormone adjustment, and that iron deficiency arising from testosterone itself or from provider-ordered phlebotomy 'remains unstudied in this population'.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the recommended response is monitoring and 'occasionally, adjustments to hormonal therapy'; no numeric threshold or phlebotomy schedule is endorsed
claims.population: Review of transgender and gender-diverse adults on gender-affirming hormone therapy, written for hematologists. This is the most direct published acknowledgment that the phlebotomy-plus-iron question in this exact population has no data behind it.
claims.quote: Although limited, the available data in the literature indicate a low thrombotic risk for transgender individuals undergoing gender-affirming testosterone therapy. However, polycythemia is a common adverse effect necessitating monitoring and, occasionally, adjustments to hormonal therapy. Additionally, iron deficiency may arise due to the physiological effects of testosterone or health care providers' use of phlebotomy, an aspect that remains unstudied in this population.

claims.statement: In the only prospective cohort of men running self-selected androgen cycles, mean hematocrit rose 0.03 L/L (about 3 percentage points) during the cycle and returned to baseline by 3 months after it ended. The rise is reversible on cessation — but a mean of +0.03 L/L conceals individual outliers, and the cohort was followed for one year only.
claims.dose: none — participants used self-selected real-world androgen cycles; this abstract reports no doses or compounds
claims.population: 100 men aged 18+ performing a self-administered androgen cycle, assessed before the cycle, at the end, at 3 months and at 1 year. This is the population closest to a self-managing TherapyLog user, and it is the only prospective data of its kind — but n=100, one cycle, one year, and the authors state the cardiovascular impact remains uncertain.
claims.quote: Mean haematocrit increased 0.03 L/L (0.02-0.03). Three months after the cycle, and 1 year after the start, these parameters returned to baseline. In conclusion, androgen abuse induces small but clinically relevant adverse changes in blood pressure, lipid metabolism and erythrocytosis which are rapidly reversible after cessation. As follow-up was limited to 1 year, the impact of androgen abuse on cardiovascular disease remains uncertain.

claims.statement: The largest cardiovascular safety trial of testosterone (5246 men, mean 21.7 months treatment) found no excess of major adverse cardiac events versus placebo — but reported a higher incidence of pulmonary embolism in the testosterone group. Reassurance on arterial events does not extend to venous ones.
claims.dose: Transdermal 1.62% testosterone gel daily, titrated to maintain serum testosterone 350-750 ng/dL; placebo-controlled, mean treatment 21.7 months
claims.population: 5246 men aged 45-80 with symptomatic hypogonadism (two fasting testosterone <300 ng/dL) and preexisting or high risk of cardiovascular disease. Transdermal gel at replacement doses — the formulation and dose least likely to cause erythrocytosis, so this trial says little about injectable or supraphysiologic use.
claims.quote: A primary cardiovascular end-point event occurred in 182 patients (7.0%) in the testosterone group and in 190 patients (7.3%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.96; 95% confidence interval, 0.78 to 1.17; P<0.001 for noninferiority). ... A higher incidence of atrial fibrillation, of acute kidney injury, and of pulmonary embolism was observed in the testosterone group.
claims.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine

claims.statement: What 17-alpha-alkylation does, in the FDA label's own words: adding a methyl group at the 17-alpha position is what makes an androgen survive oral dosing, increasing potency per unit weight versus testosterone taken by mouth. This is the structural change, not a side effect of it.
claims.dose: Methyltestosterone 10 mg to 50 mg daily orally (label: usual initial dosage in the androgen-deficient male)
claims.population: FDA US Prescribing Information for methyltestosterone tablets (Amneal, rev. 05-2025). The labelled population is adult men with confirmed primary or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism — not adults using oral androgens for physique or performance, which is off-label in every case.
claims.quote: In their active form, all drugs in the class have a 17-beta-hydroxy group. 17-alpha alkylation (methyltestosterone) increases the pharmacologic activity per unit weight compared to testosterone when given orally.

claims.statement: The label separates two different hepatic risks with two different dose relationships: peliosis hepatis and liver tumours are tied to prolonged use of HIGH doses, but cholestatic hepatitis and jaundice are stated to occur with 17-alpha-alkylandrogens at a RELATIVELY LOW dose. A 'sensible' dose is therefore not protective against the cholestatic injury.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the label asserts cholestatic hepatitis occurs 'at a relatively low dose' but names no threshold number, and names no dose or duration threshold for peliosis or neoplasm
claims.population: FDA US Prescribing Information for methyltestosterone tablets; WARNINGS section. Written for prescribed hypogonadism replacement, so it describes risk at labelled doses (10-50 mg/day), well below typical self-directed use.
claims.quote: Prolonged use of high doses of androgens has been associated with the development of peliosis hepatis and hepatic neoplasms including hepatocellular carcinoma (see PRECAUTIONS: CARCINOGENESIS, MUTAGENESIS, IMPAIRMENT OF FERTILITY ). Peliosis hepatis can be a life-threatening or fatal complication. Cholestatic hepatitis and jaundice occur with 17-alpha-alkylandrogens (such as methyltestosterone) at a relatively low dose. If cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice appears or if liver function tests become abnormal, the androgen should be discontinued and the etiology should be determined.

claims.statement: The one concrete dose threshold for hepatic dysfunction that appears on any 17-alpha-alkylated androgen label: for danazol, elevated serum enzymes and/or jaundice have been reported at daily doses of 400 mg or more. Treat this as the only labelled number of its kind, not as a general rule transferable to other compounds.
claims.dose: Danazol 400 mg/day or more (label threshold for reported hepatic dysfunction); labelled therapeutic range is 200-800 mg/day
claims.population: FDA US Prescribing Information for danazol capsules (rev. Oct 2024), ADVERSE REACTIONS. Labelled population is women with endometriosis and adults of either sex with hereditary angioedema — not people using androgens for muscle.
claims.quote: Hepatic dysfunction, as evidenced by reversible elevated serum enzymes and/or jaundice, has been reported in patients receiving a daily dosage of danazol capsules of 400 mg or more.

claims.statement: Bloodwork cannot rule out the structural liver lesions. The danazol boxed warning states that peliosis hepatis and hepatic adenoma may be silent until they cause life-threatening intra-abdominal bleeding — meaning normal LFTs are not evidence that the liver is structurally intact after long-term androgen use.
claims.dose: Danazol 200-800 mg/day per label; no dose or duration threshold is given for peliosis or adenoma
claims.population: FDA US Prescribing Information for danazol capsules, BOXED WARNING. Derived from long-term therapeutic use in endometriosis and hereditary angioedema; the label itself notes 'Experience with long-term therapy with danazol is limited.'
claims.quote: Experience with long-term therapy with danazol is limited. Peliosis hepatis and benign hepatic adenoma have been observed with long-term use. Peliosis hepatis and hepatic adenoma may be silent until complicated by acute, potentially life-threatening intraabdominal hemorrhage. The physician therefore should be alert to this possibility. Attempts should be made to determine the lowest dose that will provide adequate protection.

claims.statement: The proposed mechanism is that the 17-alpha-alkyl group slows the liver's own metabolism of the steroid, which is exactly what makes it orally bioavailable; alkylated androgens appear hepatotoxic while non-alkylated ones appear not to be. The authors state plainly that the mechanism remains poorly understood.
claims.dose: none (structural claim about the 17-alpha-alkyl substitution; no dose attached)
claims.population: Hypothesis paper in Medical Hypotheses synthesising mechanistic and animal literature on oxidative stress. No human cohort, no measured endpoint — this is a proposed mechanism, not a demonstrated one.
claims.quote: In particular, 17α-alkylated AAS appear to be hepatotoxic, whereas nonalkylated AAS appear not to be. The 17α-alkyl substitution retards hepatic metabolism of the AAS rendering it orally bioavailable. The mechanism responsible for the hepatotoxicity induced by 17α-alkylated AAS remains poorly understood.

claims.statement: A single one-hour weightlifting session raised AST and ALT significantly in healthy men and kept them elevated for at least seven days — while GGT, ALP and bilirubin stayed inside the normal range throughout. Lifting alone can produce 'liver' numbers that look pathological with no drug involved.
claims.dose: One 60-minute weightlifting programme, single bout; blood sampled repeatedly over 7 days and again at 10-12 days
claims.population: 15 healthy men accustomed to moderate physical activity but NOT to weightlifting. This is an unaccustomed-exercise model; the magnitude in a trained lifter doing a familiar session is likely smaller and was not measured here.
claims.quote: Five out of eight studied clinical chemistry parameters (AST, ALT, LD, CK and myoglobin) increased significantly after exercise (P < 0.01) and remained increased for at least 7 days postexercise. Bilirubin, gamma GT and ALP remained within the normal range.

claims.statement: In the study that founded the GGT discrimination rule, bodybuilders — both those using anabolic steroids and those not — had elevated CK, AST and ALT with GGT in the normal range, whereas hepatitis patients had all three enzymes elevated. GGT correlated with the aminotransferases only in the hepatitis group.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: self-directed anabolic steroid regimens; compounds, doses and routes were not reported in the abstract
claims.population: 15 bodybuilders taking self-directed anabolic steroids and 10 bodybuilders not taking them, compared with 49 viral hepatitis patients and 592 exercising and non-exercising medical students. Small steroid groups; a 1999 case-control design, not a prospective test of the rule.
claims.quote: In both groups of bodybuilders, CK, AST, and ALT were elevated, whereas GGT remained in the normal range. In contrast, patients with hepatitis had elevations of all three enzymes: ALT, AST, and GGT. Creatine kinase (CK) was elevated in all exercising groups. Patients with hepatitis were the only group in which a correlation was found between aminotransferases and GGT.

claims.statement: This pattern is routinely misread by clinicians. Given a written case of a steroid-using bodybuilder with high AST, ALT and CK but normal GGT, 56% of surveyed physicians never mentioned muscle as a possible source and 63% named liver disease as their primary diagnosis anyway.
claims.dose: none (survey of physicians using a written case: a 28-year-old male bodybuilder using anabolic steroids)
claims.population: 84 responding family medicine and sports medicine physicians in seven US metropolitan areas, 2001. This measures physician reasoning, not patient outcomes, and predates most of the AAS-DILI literature below.
claims.doi: none indexed — J Am Osteopath Assoc 2001;101(7):391-4 (PMID 11476029)
claims.quote: In the physician survey (n = 84 responses), 56% failed to mention muscle damage or muscle disease as a potential diagnosis, despite the markedly elevated CK level of the patient. Sixty-three percent indicated liver disease as their primary diagnosis despite normal GGT levels.
claims.journal: The Journal of the American Osteopathic Association

claims.statement: The AST/ALT ratio is time-dependent in muscle injury, which is why a single draw can mislead. In acute muscle necrosis the ratio exceeded 3, but it fell toward 1 within a few days because AST has the shorter half-life — so chronic or repeated muscle damage produces a ratio near 1 that looks hepatic.
claims.dose: none (observational; patients with muscle necrosis from extreme exercise, polymyositis or seizures)
claims.population: 16 patients with muscle necrosis and no evidence of liver disease, in three groups (extreme exercise, polymyositis, seizures). Frank rhabdomyolysis-level injury, not routine training; the ratio thresholds have never been validated in lifters on androgens.
claims.quote: All patients exhibited markedly elevated creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels consistent with muscle injury. In acute cases, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and ALT were both elevated, and the AST/ALT ratio was greater than 3, but this ratio approached 1 after a few days because of a faster decline in AST.

claims.statement: The most important limit on the GGT rule: in 18 prospectively collected cases of stanozolol liver injury, every patient had elevated total bilirubin while GGT stayed within or only slightly above normal. A normal GGT does not exclude serious 17-alpha-alkylated androgen liver injury — bilirubin is the number that moves.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: stanozolol doses not reported; all self-administered for aesthetic purposes, with poly-substance use in 10 of 18
claims.population: 18 young men aged 19-48 using stanozolol for aesthetic purposes, prospectively evaluated by the Latin American DILI Registry 2013-2023. These are people who presented with symptoms — it says nothing about how the numbers behave in asymptomatic users before that point.
claims.quote: All patients were young males aged between 19 and 48, utilizing Stanozolol for aesthetic purposes. The mean latency to symptom onset was 55 days. Predominant symptoms included jaundice and pruritus. Elevated total bilirubin levels were observed in all cases, while gamma-glutamyl transferase levels remained within or slightly above normal ranges.
claims.journal: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hepatology

claims.statement: The biochemical signature of AAS liver injury is severe jaundice with almost unremarkable enzymes: across 52 cases, peak bilirubin was 705 micromol/L while ALT peaked at 125 U/L, AST at 71 U/L and GGT at only 52 U/L, with INR 1.1 and 'bland' canalicular cholestasis on biopsy. Injury also peaked AFTER stopping — bilirubin peaked 28 days after cessation.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: self-administered AAS, most commonly methyldrostanolone; individual doses not reported
claims.population: 2 index cases plus 50 further published cases assembled in a comprehensive review, causality-graded by updated RUCAM ('possible' in 31, 'probable' in 20). A literature-assembled series, so it is skewed toward severe and publishable cases; 43% developed kidney injury.
claims.quote: The most common AAS taken was methyldrostanolone. Patients commonly present with jaundice and pruritus but may exhibit other constitutional symptoms. Patients presented 56 days after starting, and bilirubin peaked 28 days after stopping, AAS. [...] Peak values were: bilirubin 705 μmol/L, alanine transaminase 125 U/L, aspartate transaminase 71 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 262 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 52 U/L, international normalised ratio 1.1. Liver biopsies showed 'bland' canalicular cholestasis. 43% of patients developed kidney injury (peak creatinine 225 μmol/L).

claims.statement: Onset is typically around two months in, and recovery is slow: in an Australian multicentre series, median latency was 58 days from starting and median time for liver biochemistry to normalise was 175 days from presentation, with 17 of 23 hospitalised and one liver transplant. No deaths occurred.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: 40 self-sourced products across 23 patients (18 AAS, 14 SARMs, 8 bodybuilding supplements); doses not reported
claims.population: 23 patients (22/23 male, median age 30, IQR 26-42) presenting to nine Australian tertiary hospitals 2017-2023. Hospital-presenting cases only; causality was 'possible' in 17/23 and 'probable' in only 2/23, so attribution is weak by the authors' own grading.
claims.quote: Twenty-three cases of DILI were identified, involving 40 drugs: 18 AAS, 14 SARMs and eight BBS. Patients were predominantly male (22/23), with median age 30 years (IQR 26-42). Most were symptomatic (21/23). Median latency of onset was 58 days (IQR 28-112 days) from drug commencement. Most patients (17/23) were admitted to hospital. [...] Median time to normalisation of liver biochemistry was 175 days (IQR 70-292 days) from presentation.

claims.statement: 17-alpha-alkylation is not required to produce this injury. SARMs, which are non-steroidal and carry no alkyl group, cause a cholestatic syndrome described as congruent with AAS liver injury — insidious jaundice with marked hyperbilirubinaemia and only mild enzyme elevations. 'Not 17-aa' is therefore not a safety claim.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: SARMs have no approved dose anywhere; this is a review of recreational-use case reports
claims.population: Narrative literature review of published SARM DILI case reports. No cohort, no denominator, no incidence estimate — the authors state that little is known about SARM hepatotoxicity and that further study is needed.
claims.quote: SARMs have been associated with a cholestatic syndrome congruent with that of DILI from AASs, and it consists of a bland cholestasis in which there is minimal bile duct injury, inflammation, or necrosis. Patients present with an insidious onset of jaundice with marked hyperbilirubinemia and mild hepatic enzyme elevations.
claims.journal: Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology

claims.statement: The single most useful denominator: among 182 asymptomatic bodybuilders using AAS for at least six months, 38.5% had elevated liver enzymes — but CK was normal in only 27.1% of those, meaning roughly three quarters of the enzyme elevations came with a muscle signal. Toxic liver injury was diagnosed in 12.6% overall, and ultrasound found steatosis in 12.1%, one adenoma and one focal nodular hyperplasia.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: self-directed AAS use for six months or longer; compounds, doses and routes not reported in the abstract
claims.population: 182 asymptomatic male Brazilian recreational bodybuilders aged 18+, median 26 years, enrolled 2007-2012, all with clinical evaluation, abdominal ultrasound and bloods. Asymptomatic community users — the closest published population to this app's readers. Cross-sectional, so it cannot say who went on to develop injury.
claims.quote: Elevated liver enzyme levels were observed in 38.5% (n = 70) of AAS users, and creatine phosphokinase was normal in 27.1% (n = 19) of them. Hepatic steatosis was observed by AUS in 12.1% of the sample. [...] A diagnosis of toxic liver injury was suggested in 23 (12.6%) AAS users without a history of alcohol or other medications/drugs consumption, or evidence of other liver diseases.

claims.statement: A transaminase rise on an oral androgen is not proof the drug caused it. With prescribed oxandrolone at labelled doses, hepatic dysfunction appeared in 25% at 5 mg and 67% at 10 mg — but 43% of untreated burn controls also had abnormal LFTs, and the difference was not significant.
claims.dose: Oxandrolone 5 mg (n=8) or 10 mg (n=6); dosing frequency not stated in the abstract
claims.population: 14 hospitalised adult burn patients receiving oxandrolone versus 61 burn controls, single centre, retrospective. Critically ill burn patients have many competing causes of abnormal LFTs, and the groups are tiny — this shows the confounding problem, not a clean effect size.
claims.quote: Two of the eight (25%) oxandrolone patients receiving 5 mg and four of the six (67%) oxandrolone patients receiving 10 mg had evidence of hepatic dysfunction. Twenty six of the 61 (43%) control patients had evidence of hepatic dysfunction (P = NS). There appears no significant increased incidence of hepatic dysfunction in burn patients who received oxandrolone compared to those who did not.

claims.statement: Even under prescribed, monitored use, transaminitis on an oral 17-alpha-alkylated androgen is common and early: 41.4% of 309 adult burn patients on oxandrolone crossed AST or ALT above 100 U/L, at a median of 13 days on drug. The authors note that monitoring requirements for this are still not established.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: oxandrolone dose not reported in the abstract (multicentre retrospective; standard-of-care burn dosing)
claims.population: 309 adult burn inpatients across multiple US burn centres. Hospitalised, critically ill, on many concomitant drugs — vasopressor and amiodarone use were independent predictors — so the incidence is not transferable to a healthy adult self-dosing at home.
claims.quote: A total of 309 patients were included, with transaminitis occurring in 128 patients (41.4%) after 13 (interquartile range [IQR] 8-23) days on oxandrolone. After multivariable analysis, age (odds ratio [OR] 0.91; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84-0.99 for a 5-year increase in age), intravenous vasopressor use (OR 1.85; 95% CI 1.05-3.27), and amiodarone use (OR 2.51; 95% CI 1.09-5.77) were independent predictors of transaminitis, controlling for TBSA%.

claims.statement: The reference range most labs print is too generous. In a healthy blood-donor population screened for liver disease, updated healthy upper limits were 30 U/L for men and 19 U/L for women, versus the conventional 40 and 30 U/L — and ALT tracked BMI and metabolic markers independently.
claims.dose: none (reference-interval study; no drug administered)
claims.population: 6,835 first-time blood donors in Milan, 1995-1999, anti-HCV negative, validated against 209 anti-HCV-positive donors. Sedentary healthy adults, NOT people who lift — Pettersson (PMID 17764474) shows a single lifting session moves ALT for a week, so these limits are not a resting baseline for a trained population.
claims.quote: Serum ALT activity was independently related to body mass index and to laboratory indicators of abnormal lipid or carbohydrate metabolism. Updated upper limits (for men, 500 nkat/L [30 U/L]; for women, 317 nkat/L [19 U/L]) were lower than current limits (for men, 667 nkat/L [40 U/L]; for women, 500 nkat/L [30 U/L])

claims.statement: Results are not comparable across labs. The upper limit of normal for ALT still varies roughly two-fold between institutions — from 30 to 60 U/L — because of different reference populations and different analysers. A number logged from one lab cannot be trended against a number from another without knowing both reference ranges.
claims.dose: none (assay and reference-interval review)
claims.population: Review of laboratory reference-range practice across institutions; general clinical chemistry, not specific to androgen users. The authors conclude that standardisation remains an unmet need.
claims.quote: There are considerable differences in the values for what constitutes a 'normal' ALT serum concentration set by laboratories, and reference values may vary two-fold between different institutions (from 30 to 60 U/l).
