Key reasons for this include using markedly different reference populations to establish the bounds of normal, and differences in analyzers and assays used to quantify ALT levels.

claims.statement: The counterweight, stated by the authors themselves: controlled studies in athletes did not find liver damage from AAS — but the same review warns those studies used doses far below what people actually take, so the literature probably understates real-world harm. Both halves have to travel together.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the review notes administered study doses 'do not approximate doses used by illicit steroid users'; specific doses not given in the abstract
claims.population: Narrative review of the laboratory and field literature on AAS in athletes. The 'no liver damage' finding comes from short-term controlled administration studies at low doses, many using injectable non-alkylated esters — the population and the compounds both differ from oral 17-alpha-alkylated use.
claims.quote: In studies of athletes, AAS were not found to damage the liver. [...] One has to keep in mind that the scientific data may underestimate the actual untoward effects because of the relatively low doses administered in those studies, since they do not approximate doses used by illicit steroid users.

claims.statement: Cabergoline's only FDA-approved use is hyperprolactinemic disorders (idiopathic or due to pituitary adenoma) in adults, and the approved dose ceiling is 1 mg twice weekly — 2 mg/week total. A man taking cabergoline without documented true hyperprolactinaemia is outside the indication entirely; a man above 2 mg/week is above the approved ceiling even if his prolactin is genuinely raised.
claims.dose: 0.25 mg orally twice weekly to start; titrate by 0.25 mg twice weekly no more often than every 4 weeks; maximum 1 mg orally twice weekly (2 mg/week)
claims.population: Adults with hyperprolactinemic disorders, idiopathic or from pituitary adenoma. Safety database: 'more than 900 patients with hyperprolactinemic disorders'. Not studied in men using exogenous androgens, peptides or performance compounds.
claims.pmid: n/a — FDA US Prescribing Information (DailyMed setid e497366b-a124-4d7f-bd45-a883c392d4bb), published Jun 30, 2026
claims.quote: CABERGOLINE is an ergot derivative indicated for the treatment of hyperprolactinemic disorders, either idiopathic or due to pituitary adenomas in adults. […] The recommended starting dosage of CABERGOLINE is 0.25 mg orally twice weekly. Titrate CABERGOLINE to achieve normal serum prolactin levels by increasing CABERGOLINE by 0.25 mg orally twice weekly at intervals of no less than 4 weeks. The maximum recommended dosage is 1 mg orally, twice weekly

claims.statement: The current US label requires an echocardiogram BEFORE the first dose, not just during treatment, and requires repeat echocardiography every 6 to 12 months while on the drug. This is the single most consequential gap between the label and how cabergoline is typically obtained and used outside a clinic — most community use begins with no baseline echo, which means any later valve finding cannot be attributed to the drug or excluded as pre-existing.
claims.dose: Baseline echocardiogram before initiation; surveillance echocardiogram every 6 to 12 months or as clinically indicated
claims.population: All adults prescribed cabergoline for hyperprolactinemic disorders
claims.pmid: n/a — FDA US Prescribing Information (DailyMed setid e497366b-a124-4d7f-bd45-a883c392d4bb), published Jun 30, 2026
claims.quote: Before initiating CABERGOLINE evaluate for valvular heart disease, including with an echocardiogram. If valvular disease is detected, do not administer CABERGOLINE. […] During CABERGOLINE treatment, monitor for the development of valvulopathy with a cardiac echocardiogram at intervals of 6 to 12 months or as clinically indicated and monitor for chest pain and signs and symptoms of heart failure

claims.statement: Cabergoline is contraindicated — not merely cautioned — in uncontrolled hypertension, in anyone with a history of cardiac valvular disorder or pericardial fibrosis, and in anyone with a history of pleural, pulmonary or retroperitoneal fibrotic disease. Uncontrolled hypertension is a realistic exclusion in men using androgens or stimulants. The label also carries a specific warning for impulse control disorders and compulsive behaviours.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: this is a contraindication and warning statement, not a dose
claims.population: All adults prescribed cabergoline
claims.pmid: n/a — FDA US Prescribing Information (DailyMed setid e497366b-a124-4d7f-bd45-a883c392d4bb), published Jun 30, 2026
claims.quote: CABERGOLINE is contraindicated in patients with: • Uncontrolled hypertension. • Known hypersensitivity to ergot derivatives. • History of cardiac valvular disorders, as suggested by anatomical evidence of valvulopathy of any valve, determined by pre-treatment evaluation including echocardiographic demonstration of valve leaflet thickening, valve restriction, or mixed valve restriction-stenosis, or history of pericardial fibrosis […] • History of pleural, pulmonary, or retroperitoneal fibrotic disorders

claims.statement: In actual prolactinoma practice, the doses that resolve resistant disease sit well above the label ceiling: in a prospective study of 150 patients, the mean weekly dose at prolactin normalisation was 5.2 mg/week in the cabergoline-resistant group, and control in poor responders needed more than 3 mg/week. This is the clinical justification for high-dose use — it exists for tumour control, not for cosmetic prolactin lowering, and it is the same dose range that drives cumulative-exposure concerns.
claims.dose: Mean weekly dose at prolactin normalisation: 2.0 ± 0.3 mg/week (untreated), 0.9 ± 0.1 mg/week (previously intolerant), 5.2 ± 0.6 mg/week (resistant); >3 mg/week required in poor responders
claims.population: 150 prolactinoma patients (122 women, 28 men; 93 microadenomas, 57 macroadenomas), 47 post-transsphenoidal surgery, treated for 1 year
claims.quote: Mean cabergoline dose in milligrams per week at the time of prolactin normalization was 2.0 +/- 0.3 in group U, 0.9 +/- 0.1 in group I, and 5.2 +/- 0.6 in group R. Prolactin normalization rate at the 3 mg/wk dose was 84% overall but only 35% in group R. […] Hyperprolactinemia could be controlled in poor responders within 1 yr with doses higher than 3 mg/wk.

claims.statement: For the group closest to a man with a genuinely raised prolactin and a normal pituitary MRI, the maintenance dose that actually worked was 0.25 mg ONCE weekly — a quarter of the label's starting dose and a twentieth of the resistant-prolactinoma dose. All 13 men normalised prolactin and testosterone; none needed surgery. If a dose is being taken above this in the absence of a tumour, the study base does not support it.
claims.dose: Median maintenance cabergoline 0.25 mg per week (one 0.25 mg dose weekly), sustained over a mean 72-month follow-up
claims.population: 13 men with true (PEG-confirmed) hyperprolactinaemia and normal pituitary MRI; mean age 51 ± 16 y (range 20-77); mean prolactin 91 ng/mL (range 28-264); 8 of 13 with low baseline testosterone
claims.quote: Mean age at diagnosis was 51 ± 16 years (range, 20-77); mean serum prolactin level at presentation was 91 ng/ml (range, 28-264), eight men presented with low baseline testosterone. […] Currently, after a mean follow-up of 72 months, ten patients continue treatment with caborgoline (median weekly dose, 0.25 mg), whereas three men discontinued treatment.

claims.statement: The strongest positive valvulopathy signal in hyperprolactinaemia comes from the CATCH study, which put a number on it: cumulative cabergoline exposure above 115 mg was associated with roughly nine-fold higher adjusted odds of having two or more valves with grade 2+ regurgitation, versus bromocriptine. At 1 mg/week, 115 mg cumulative is reached in about 2.2 years; at 0.5 mg/week, about 4.4 years. The abnormalities found were 'primarily mild', and this is cross-sectional, not outcome, data.
claims.dose: Cumulative cabergoline exposure >115 mg (median exposure duration 2.8 years in cabergoline-only users)
claims.population: 174 asymptomatic community-based adults (mean age 49 ± 13 y, 63% women, so only ~64 men) on a dopamine agonist >12 months for hyperprolactinaemia, with no known structural heart disease before therapy; 62 cabergoline only, 63 bromocriptine only, 49 both
claims.quote: Cumulative cabergoline exposure > 115 mg was associated with a higher age-sex adjusted odds of ≥2 valves with grade 2+ regurgitation (aOR 9.6, 95%CI:1.1-81.3, P = 0.04) compared to bromocriptine only. Among community-based adults treated for hyperprolactinemia, cabergoline use and greater cumulative cabergoline exposure were associated with a higher prevalence of primarily mild valvular regurgitation compared with bromocriptine.

claims.statement: The largest cross-sectional echocardiographic study contradicts the cumulative-dose signal: in 747 UK patients at a median cumulative cabergoline dose of 152 mg — above CATCH's 115 mg threshold — there was no association between cumulative dose and valvular abnormality, and only 3.2% had moderate stenosis or regurgitation of any kind.
claims.dose: Median cumulative cabergoline dose 152 mg (IQR 50-348 mg)
claims.population: 747 patients (251 males, one third) on dopamine agonists for lactotrope pituitary tumours across 28 UK endocrine centres; median age 42 y (IQR 34-52); 601 on cabergoline alone
claims.quote: The median cumulative dose for cabergoline was 152 mg (IQR, 50-348 mg), and for bromocriptine it was 7815 mg (IQR, 1764-20 477 mg). A total of 28 cases of moderate valvular stenosis or regurgitation were observed in 24 (3.2%) patients. No associations were observed between cumulative doses of dopamine agonist used and the age-corrected prevalence of any valvular abnormality.

claims.statement: The only prospective study with baseline and follow-up echocardiograms on the same equipment found no clinically relevant valve change at a median cumulative dose of 277.8 mg over a median 124.5 months (roughly 10 years) of treatment. This is the best-designed reassurance available, and it reaches nearly 2.5x the CATCH threshold without a signal.
claims.dose: Median cumulative total cabergoline dose 277.8 mg (IQR 121.4-437.8 mg); median total treatment duration 124.5 months
claims.population: 100 patients (71 female, so 29 men) with prolactinoma (n=89) or idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia (n=11); median age at diagnosis 41.5 y; median 62.5 months between baseline and last echo
claims.quote: The median total duration of cabergoline treatment was 124.5 months (interquartile range: 80.75-188.75) and the median cumulative total dose of cabergoline was 277.8 mg (interquartile range : 121.4-437.8 mg) at last follow-up. We found no clinically relevant alterations in cardiac valve function or valvular calcifications with cabergoline treatment.

claims.statement: When the endpoint is events people actually care about — valve surgery or heart failure — rather than echo findings, low-dose cabergoline shows no excess risk. In 646 primary-care prolactinoma patients at a median cumulative dose of 56 mg and a median 2.1 mg/week (the label ceiling), the relative risk of a hard cardiac endpoint was 0.78 versus matched controls, and re-reading the echoes of affected patients showed no ergot-pattern valvulopathy.
claims.dose: Median cumulative dose 56 mg (IQR 27-123); median weekly dose 2.1 mg; median treatment duration 27 months (IQR 15-46)
claims.population: 646 patients on cabergoline >6 months for prolactinoma, drawn from ~1.5 million North East London primary care records, each matched to up to 5 controls on age, gender, ethnicity, location, diabetes, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and smoking
claims.quote: Median cumulative cabergoline dose was 56 mg (interquartile range [IQR] 27-123). Median treatment duration was 27 months (IQR 15-46). Median weekly dose was 2.1 mg. Neither univariate nor multivariate analysis demonstrated a significant association between cabergoline treatment at any cumulative dosage/duration and an increased incidence of cardiac endpoints. In a matched analysis, the relative risk for cardiac complications in the cabergoline-treated group was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.41-1.48; P = 0.446).

claims.statement: 'Low dose' is not automatically safe over long enough time. A documented case developed aortic and mitral valve thickening and regurgitation on 0.5-1 mg weekly after 15 years (cumulative 572 mg), which then worsened over three further years (cumulative 649 mg). The weekly dose stayed at or below the label ceiling throughout; it was duration, not intensity, that accumulated. This is a single case and cannot establish rate — but it does establish that the pattern is possible.
claims.dose: 0.5-1 mg weekly, continuous for 18 years; valve changes documented at 572 mg cumulative, worse at 649 mg cumulative
claims.population: One 60-year-old man with prolactinoma, initially on bromocriptine for 5 years, then switched to cabergoline; case report
claims.quote: After a 15-year-course of cabergoline therapy with a cumulative dose of 572 mg, echocardiographic monitoring demonstrated aortic and mitral valve thickening and regurgitation. An additional 3 years of cabergoline treatment (cumulative dose: 649 mg) resulted in worsening valve thickening and regurgitation. […] We report a case of mitral and aortic vavulopathy in a patient who was treated with long-term (18 years) low-dosage (.5-1 mg weekly) cabergoline.

claims.statement: Four reversible or benign causes should be excluded BEFORE either a macroprolactin assay or pituitary MRI is ordered: pregnancy, drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia, primary hypothyroidism, and renal failure. For this app's readers the drug list is the live one — antipsychotics, antiemetics such as metoclopramide and domperidone, some antidepressants, and opioids all raise prolactin, and no amount of cabergoline addresses the actual cause.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: this is a diagnostic sequencing statement, not a dose
claims.population: General hyperprolactinaemic population; narrative review of diagnostic pitfalls
claims.quote: Before submitting patients to macroprolactin screening and pituitary magnetic resonance imaging, one should rule out pregnancy, drug-induced hyperprolactinemia, primary hypothyroidism, and renal failure. The magnitude of PRL elevation can be useful in determining the etiology of hyperprolactinemia.

claims.statement: The magnitude of the prolactin number guides whether imaging is warranted. Above 250 ng/mL, a prolactinoma is highly likely and non-functioning adenomas are effectively excluded. Below 100 ng/mL, most cases are non-functioning adenoma, drug effect, macroprolactinaemia or systemic disease — though up to 25% of microprolactinomas also fall below 100. Separately, a normal-or-mildly-raised prolactin alongside a large (≥3 cm) pituitary mass is a trap: the 'hook effect' can report a falsely low value, unmasked only by repeating the assay at 1:100 dilution.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: diagnostic thresholds — PRL >250 ng/mL highly suggestive of prolactinoma; PRL ≤250 ng/mL with a ≥3 cm adenoma should trigger a 1:100 dilution to exclude hook effect
claims.population: General hyperprolactinaemic population; narrative review of diagnostic pitfalls
claims.quote: PRL values >250 ng/mL are highly suggestive of prolactinomas and virtually exclude nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas (NFPAs) and other sellar masses as the etiology of hyperprolactinemia. […] Falsely low PRL levels may result from the so-called "hook effect," which should be considered in all cases of large (≥3 cm) pituitary adenomas associated with normal or mildly elevated PRL levels (≤250 ng/mL). The hook effect may be unmasked by repeating PRL measurement after a 1:100 serum sample dilution.

claims.statement: The hook effect disproportionately affects men — 70% of published cases were male — and the clinical picture gives no warning, because hook-effect macroprolactinomas look like macroprolactinomas that do not hook. In these cases the mean prolactin reported before dilution was 108 ng/mL; after dilution it was over 38,000 ng/mL. A man with visual symptoms or headaches and an unimpressive prolactin has not been cleared by that number.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: dilution studies of prolactin recommended in all patients with a pituitary macroadenoma and normal or mildly elevated prolactin; smallest hooking tumour had a largest dimension of 2.9 cm
claims.population: 61 macroprolactinoma patients demonstrating the hook effect, pooled from case reports, case series and observational studies to April 2024 plus institutional cases; mean age 40.0 ± 15.7 y; 70% male
claims.quote: Seventy percent of the patients were male. The smallest reported macroprolactinoma volume demonstrating the hook effect was 3.4 cm³ with its largest dimension measuring 2.9 cm. Mean pre- and postdilution serum prolactin levels were 108.1 ng/mL and 38 526.9 ng/mL, respectively. […] Clinical characteristics of macroprolactinomas that demonstrate the hook effect greatly resemble those that do not, underscoring the need to perform dilution studies of prolactin in all patients with pituitary macroadenomas with normal or mildly elevated serum prolactin.

claims.statement: Macroprolactin — prolactin bound in a large, biologically inactive complex — accounts for somewhere between 4% and 40% of raised prolactin results depending on the population tested. Critically, symptoms do NOT distinguish it: macroprolactinaemic patients present with the same low libido, ED and galactorrhoea picture. Failing to test for it leads directly to unnecessary imaging and unnecessary drug treatment. Standard immunoassays do not correct for it; the test is polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, which most labs will only run on request.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: PEG precipitation is a laboratory test, not a dose. No commercially available prolactin assay is free of macroprolactin interference.
claims.population: Hyperprolactinaemic patients across referral populations; AACE/ACE systematic review of the macroprolactin literature to October 2014
claims.quote: MacroPRL is an under-recognized cause of elevated prolactin (PRL) and is present in approximately 4% to 40% of hyperprolactinemic patients depending on the referral population. […] Because of this there is significant overlap in the clinical presentation of patients with true hyperprolactinemia and those with macroPRL, differentiation cannot always be made on the basis of symptoms. A lack of recognition of the presence of macroPRL can lead to unnecessary laboratory investigations, imaging, and pharmacologic or surgical treatment. Until there is a commercially available PRL assay that is not subject to interference by macroPRL, clinicians should consider the possibility of macroPRL, especially if the clinical presentation, imaging findings, and/or response to therapy reveal inconsistencies.

claims.statement: Macroprolactinaemia is not a rare curiosity — it is the third most common cause of non-physiological hyperprolactinaemia after drugs and prolactinomas, and up to 40% of people with it have hypogonadal symptoms, infertility or galactorrhoea. That combination is exactly why symptom-plus-number reasoning fails here: the symptoms that prompt the test are present in the group for whom the number is an artefact.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: screening recommendation, not a dose — macroprolactin screening indicated both for asymptomatic subjects and for those without an obvious cause for prolactin elevation
claims.population: General hyperprolactinaemic population; narrative review of diagnostic pitfalls
claims.quote: Currently, macroprolactinemia is the third most frequent cause of nonphysiological hyperprolactinemia after drugs and prolactinomas. Up to 40% of macroprolactinemic patients may present with hypogonadism symptoms, infertility, and/or galactorrhea. Thus, the screening for macroprolactin is indicated not only for asymptomatic subjects but also for those without an obvious cause for their prolactin (PRL) elevation.

claims.statement: The one adequately-sized randomised trial of cabergoline for erectile dysfunction in men NOT selected for hyperprolactinaemia found a modest effect: 0.5-1 mg weekly for 6 months produced a positive clinical result in 31.2% versus 7.1% on placebo, in sildenafil non-responders. The trade was real — significantly more adverse effects on cabergoline and 5.9% had to stop the drug. The authors explicitly declined to draw final conclusions. This is the closest thing to evidence for the community sexual-function use, and it is thin.
claims.dose: 0.5-1 mg cabergoline weekly for 6 months
claims.population: 402 men aged 21-59 who had failed sildenafil, randomised to cabergoline or placebo; 370 (92%) completed. Not selected for raised prolactin; baseline prolactin was measured but no hyperprolactinaemia entry criterion is stated in the abstract.
claims.quote: Patients were randomly divided into group 1, those who received 0.5-1 mg cabergoline weekly for 6 months and group 2, who received placebo for the same period. […] Positive clinical results were seen in 31.2% of patients in the cabergoline group compared with 7.1% of patients in the placebo group (P=0.04). […] More drug-related adverse effects occurred in cabergoline group and 12 (5.9%) had to discontinue treatment (P=0.001). Cabergoline is moderately effective salvage therapy for sildenafil nonresponse. Further studies with different dosages and treatment regimens are necessary to draw final conclusions on the efficacy of this drug in ED.

claims.statement: In hyperprolactinaemic men, the sexual benefit of cabergoline tracked prolactin normalisation almost perfectly — objectively measured overnight erections normalised in 60.6% of men whose prolactin normalised but only 7.7% of those whose prolactin did not. The mechanism is prolactin correction, not a direct dopaminergic sexual effect. That is the argument against expecting benefit in a man whose prolactin was never elevated.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the abstract reports 6 months of cabergoline treatment without stating the dose used
claims.population: 51 consecutive hyperprolactinaemic men (41 macroprolactinomas, 10 microprolactinomas) vs 51 healthy male controls; erectile function measured objectively by nocturnal penile tumescence
claims.quote: After 6 months of cabergoline treatment, prolactin levels normalized in 74.5% of patients: 73.2% of macroprolactinomas and 80% of microprolactinomas. Testosterone levels normalized in 68.6% of patients, whereas NPT normalized in 60.6% of patients who had normalized prolactin levels and in 7.7% of patients who did not.

claims.statement: Impulse control disorders are the most under-discussed cabergoline harm in men. In a series of eight hypogonadal men with prolactinomas and no prior psychiatric history, every one developed disruptive hypersexuality on dopamine agonist therapy — at various doses, with cabergoline, bromocriptine and quinagolide all implicated. Consequences included relationship breakdown, financial loss and illicit activity. The authors propose the mechanism is dopamine reward-pathway stimulation combined with rapid restoration of a eugonadal state after prolonged hypogonadism — a combination that describes a large share of this app's readership.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: hypersexuality occurred 'at various doses'; no threshold dose is identified. Screening in the first six months of therapy is suggested.
claims.population: 8 men with prolactinoma and associated central hypogonadism, no prior psychiatric disease, multicentre retrospective cohort
claims.quote: The eight men had no prior history of psychiatric disease, but each developed disruptive hypersexuality whilst on dopamine agonist therapy at various doses. Cabergoline, bromocriptine and quinagolide were all implicated. Hypersexuality had manifold consequences, including relationship discord, financial loss, reduced work performance, and illicit activity. We hypothesise that this phenomenon is due to synergy between reward pathway stimulation by dopamine agonists, together with rapid restoration of the eugonadal state after prolonged hypogonadism.

claims.statement: When systematically asked, over half of dopamine-agonist-treated pituitary patients report at least one impulse control disorder: 28.5% compulsive shopping, 24.5% punding, 24.5% hypersexuality, with 19% reporting two or three types. Independent risk factors were younger age, being single, and a history of psychiatric illness. Note the design limit — this is a questionnaire prevalence, not an incidence attributable to the drug, and a 12-week prospective study at 0.40 mg/week found no increase. The honest reading is that the risk is real, common enough to warrant asking about, and poorly quantified.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: cross-sectional prevalence across mixed dopamine agonists and doses; no dose-response reported
claims.population: 200 patients with prolactinoma or non-functioning pituitary adenoma on dopamine agonists, followed at tertiary referral centres; multicentre cross-sectional
claims.quote: At least one ICD was reported by 52% of participants, among whom 28.5% mentioned compulsive shopping, 24.5% punding, and 24.5% hypersexuality. Furthermore, 33% of the patients reported the presence of one type of ICD behavior, while 12% specified two and 7% had three types of such behavior. The multivariable logistic regression showed that the significant risk factors of ICD were younger age (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]: 0.92, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.88-0.97, p 0.001), being single (AOR: 0.15, 95%CI: 0.03-0.84, p 0.03), and a positive history of psychiatric illness (AOR: 7.67, 95% CI: 1.37-42.97, p 0.021).

claims.statement: If hyperprolactinaemia really is the cause of a man's low testosterone, correcting the prolactin usually fixes the testosterone on its own — 69% recovered normal testosterone without replacement — but it can take time, with half of those who recovered doing so a median 6.5 months AFTER prolactin normalised. Higher baseline testosterone predicted recovery. Practically: do not judge whether cabergoline 'worked' on a testosterone drawn weeks after prolactin normalises, and note that patients started on testosterone replacement within 6 months were excluded, so this recovery cannot be observed in someone already on exogenous androgens.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: outcome study of prolactin normalisation; cabergoline dose not reported in the abstract
claims.population: 29 men with central hypogonadism and successfully treated isolated hyperprolactinaemia (23 prolactinoma, 5 stalk effect from non-functioning adenoma, 1 idiopathic); median age 50 y (IQR 41-58). Men given testosterone replacement within 6 months of prolactin normalisation were excluded.
claims.quote: After successful treatment of hyperprolactinemia, 20 patients (69%) spontaneously recovered the gonadal axis, achieving normal TT levels. Ten patients normalized PRL and TT values concurrently, while the other 10 exhibited a median delay of 6.5 months (4-9.25) after PRL normalization; the former group showed lower baseline PRL levels at diagnosis compared to the latter (p = 0.007). Patients who recovered the gonadal axis had higher baseline TT values compared to those with persistent hypogonadism (p = 0.02).

claims.statement: Prolactin does appear elevated in men using anabolic-androgenic steroids, but the evidence is two very small uncontrolled cross-sectional studies with mixed compounds and no dose data — nowhere near enough to establish which compound raises prolactin, by how much, whether it is clinically meaningful, or whether treating it with cabergoline changes anything. In the Saudi athlete series, 10 AAS users versus 6 non-users showed significantly increased prolactin alongside suppressed LH and FSH. Treat this as a signal worth measuring, not a reason to pre-emptively dose a dopamine agonist.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: no cabergoline was used; AAS type, dose and course length were self-reported and not reported quantitatively in the abstract
claims.population: 16 male Saudi athletes — 10 AAS users, 6 non-users. Very small, cross-sectional, self-reported compound use, no adjustment for confounders.
claims.quote: Total testosterone increased significantly among AAS (.05), along with a significant decrease in LH (.01), and FSH ( 0.001) levels, while serum prolactin and estradiol levels were significantly increased ( 0.05).

claims.statement: Finasteride 1 mg once daily is the FDA-approved dose for male pattern hair loss, and the label itself sets the timeline: at least three months before any benefit is visible, continued use required to hold it, and full reversal of effect within 12 months of stopping.
claims.dose: 1 mg orally once daily
claims.population: Men with male pattern hair loss. The label excludes women entirely and states efficacy in bitemporal recession has not been established — so hairline-only loss and any use in women are outside the approved indication.
claims.quote: The recommended dose of PROPECIA is one tablet (1 mg) taken once daily. In general, daily use for three months or more is necessary before benefit is observed. Continued use is recommended to sustain benefit, which should be re-evaluated periodically. Withdrawal of treatment leads to reversal of effect within 12 months.

claims.statement: Isoform coverage, from the label: finasteride is ~100-fold selective for Type II 5-alpha-reductase (IC50 4.2 nM) over Type I (IC50 500 nM). Type II supplies about two-thirds of circulating DHT and is the isoform in hair follicles; Type I supplies about one-third and is the isoform predominant in scalp sebaceous glands. This is the mechanistic basis for the claim that a dual inhibitor covers more of the pathway.
claims.dose: none — mechanism and enzyme-selectivity claim, not a dosing claim
claims.population: Humans; in vitro binding studies used native human scalp and prostate tissue.
claims.quote: In humans, Type I 5α-reductase is predominant in the sebaceous glands of most regions of skin, including scalp, and liver. Type I 5α-reductase is responsible for approximately one-third of circulating DHT. The Type II 5α-reductase isozyme is primarily found in prostate, seminal vesicles, epididymides, and hair follicles as well as liver, and is responsible for two-thirds of circulating DHT. In humans, the mechanism of action of finasteride is based on its preferential inhibition of the Type II isozyme. Using native tissues (scalp and prostate), in vitro binding studies examining the potential of finasteride to inhibit either isozyme revealed a 100-fold selectivity for the human Type II 5α-reductase over Type I isozyme (IC 50 =500 and 4.2 nM for Type I and II, respectively).

claims.statement: Finasteride 5 mg/day suppresses serum DHT by approximately 70% sustained over four years, with maximum effect 8 hours after the first dose. Median testosterone rises about 10-20% but stays within the physiologic range — the label does not describe finasteride as raising testosterone out of range.
claims.dose: 5 mg/day (BPH dose; note this is 5x the hair-loss dose)
claims.population: Men with symptomatic BPH, dosed up to 4 years. Not men taking the 1 mg hair-loss dose.
claims.journal: FDA US Prescribing Information (finasteride 5 mg), section 12.2
claims.quote: In man, a single 5 mg oral dose of finasteride produces a rapid reduction in serum DHT concentration, with the maximum effect observed 8 hours after the first dose. The suppression of DHT is maintained throughout the 24-hour dosing interval and with continued treatment. Daily dosing of finasteride at 5 mg/day for up to 4 years has been shown to reduce the serum DHT concentration by approximately 70%. The median circulating level of testosterone increased by approximately 10 to 20% but remained within the physiologic range.

claims.statement: Dutasteride inhibits BOTH type 1 and type 2 5-alpha-reductase, and the DHT suppression is both faster and deeper than finasteride's: 85% at one week, 90% at two weeks, 94% at one year, 95% at three and four years. Maximum effect on DHT is reached within 1-2 weeks — this is a DHT timeline, not a hair-growth timeline.
claims.dose: 0.5 mg/day
claims.population: Men with BPH (the population studied for these pharmacodynamic figures), dosed up to 4 years.
claims.journal: FDA US Prescribing Information (dutasteride), sections 12.1 and 12.2
claims.quote: Dutasteride is a competitive and specific inhibitor of both type 1 and type 2 5 alpha-reductase isoenzymes, with which it forms a stable enzyme complex. [...] The maximum effect of daily doses of dutasteride on the reduction of DHT is dose dependent and is observed within 1 to 2 weeks. After 1 and 2 weeks of daily dosing with dutasteride 0.5 mg, median serum DHT concentrations were reduced by 85% and 90%, respectively. In patients with BPH treated with dutasteride 0.5 mg/day for 4 years, the median decrease in serum DHT was 94% at 1 year, 93% at 2 years, and 95% at both 3 and 4 years.

claims.statement: Two facts from the dutasteride label that matter to anyone self-tracking labs or donating blood: dutasteride halves serum PSA within 3-6 months (so a 'normal' PSA on dutasteride may not be normal), and the label imposes a 6-month blood donation deferral after the last dose. The label also carries a high-grade prostate cancer warning.
claims.dose: 0.5 mg/day (the approved BPH dose; the same dose used off-label for hair)
claims.population: Men taking dutasteride for BPH. The PSA effect and donation deferral apply on pharmacology, not on indication — they hold for off-label hair-loss use too.
claims.quote: Dutasteride reduces serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) concentration by approximately 50%. However, any confirmed increase in PSA while on dutasteride capsules may signal the presence of prostate cancer and should be evaluated, even if those values are still within the normal range for untreated men. ( 5.1 ) Dutasteride may increase the risk of high-grade prostate cancer. ( 5.2 , 6.1 ) [...] Patients should not donate blood until 6 months after their last dose of dutasteride. ( 5.5 )

claims.statement: The OTC 5% minoxidil solution label sets 1 mL twice daily, states explicitly that more or more-often does not improve results, gives a 2-to-4-month time to visible effect, and — importantly — states that regrowth has not been shown to last beyond 48 weeks in the large trials.
claims.dose: 1 mL of 5% topical solution, twice daily, to the vertex
claims.population: Men aged 18 and over with vertex hair loss. The label excludes women, under-18s, frontal baldness and receding hairline, and directs anyone with heart disease to ask a doctor first.
claims.pmid: n/a — FDA OTC label (DailyMed setid acc5ad74-4558-4be9-aab4-94ad9ddad6b2)
claims.journal: FDA OTC Drug Label (Minoxidil Topical Solution, 5%)
claims.quote: apply one mL with dropper 2 times a day directly onto the scalp in the hair loss area using more or more often will not improve results continued use is necessary to increase and keep your hair regrowth, or hair loss will begin again [...] hair regrowth has not been shown to last longer than 48 weeks in large clinical trials with continuous treatment with 5% minoxidil topical solution for men [...] it takes time to regrow hair. Results may occur at 2 months with twice a day usage. For some men, you may need to use this product for at least 4 months before you see results.

claims.statement: Finasteride's DHT suppression plateaus well below 1 mg: in a 42-day dose-ranging biopsy study, 0.2 mg/day already produced near-maximal scalp-skin (56.5%) and serum (68.6%) DHT reduction, with 1 mg (64.1% scalp, 71.4% serum) and 5 mg (69.4% scalp, 72.2% serum) adding little. Note this study measured DHT, not hair counts — it does not establish that 0.2 mg grows as much hair as 1 mg.
claims.dose: 0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 1 or 5 mg/day for 42 days
claims.population: 249 men with androgenetic alopecia, scalp-biopsied before and after 42 days.
claims.doi: not assigned in the PubMed record — cite as PMID 10495374, J Am Acad Dermatol 1999;41(4):550-4, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10495374/
claims.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
claims.quote: Scalp skin DHT levels declined significantly by 13.0% with placebo and by 14.9%, 61.6%, 56. 5%, 64.1%, and 69.4% with 0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 1, and 5 mg doses of finasteride, respectively. Serum DHT levels declined significantly (P <.001) by 49.5%, 68.6%, 71.4%, and 72.2% in the 0.05, 0.2, 1, and 5 mg finasteride treatment groups, respectively.

claims.statement: Head-to-head, dutasteride 0.5 mg/day beat finasteride 1 mg/day on hair count and hair width at 24 weeks in 917 men, with adverse events similar across groups. The hard limit: the trial ran only 24 weeks, so it says nothing about whether that advantage holds over the years people actually take these drugs.
claims.dose: Dutasteride 0.02, 0.1 or 0.5 mg/day versus finasteride 1 mg/day versus placebo, 24 weeks
claims.population: 917 randomized men aged 20-50 with androgenetic alopecia (phase III, multicentre). No women; no one over 50.
claims.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
claims.quote: Men aged 20 to 50 years with androgenetic alopecia were randomized to receive dutasteride (0.02, 0.1, or 0.5 mg/d), finasteride (1 mg/d), or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary end point was hair count (2.54-cm diameter) at week 24. ... Hair count and width increased dose dependently with dutasteride. Dutasteride 0.5 mg significantly increased hair count and width in a 2.54-cm diameter and improved hair growth (frontal view; panel photographic assessment) at week 24 compared with finasteride (P = .003, P = .004, and P = .002, respectively) and placebo (all P < .001). The number and severity of adverse events were similar among treatment groups. The study was limited to 24 weeks.

claims.statement: Topical finasteride achieved hair counts numerically similar to oral finasteride while cutting serum DHT by only 34.5% versus 55.6% for oral, with peak plasma finasteride more than 100-fold lower. This is the central quantitative argument for topical as a lower-systemic-exposure route — but the trial was not powered to show a difference in sexual adverse events, and the authors phrase the benefit as 'less likelihood', not a demonstrated reduction.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the retrieved abstract does not state the topical finasteride concentration or the volume applied, so the exact dose behind the 34.5% DHT figure is not recoverable from the abstract
claims.population: 458 randomized adult male outpatients with androgenetic alopecia at 45 European sites; 323 completed, 446 evaluable for safety. 24 weeks.
claims.journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
claims.quote: Change from baseline in target area hair count (TAHC) at week 24 (primary efficacy endpoint) was significantly greater with topical finasteride than placebo (adjusted mean change 20.2 vs. 6.7 hairs; P < 0.001), and numerically similar between topical and oral finasteride. ... As maximum plasma finasteride concentrations were >100 times lower, and reduction from baseline in mean serum DHT concentration was lower (34.5 vs. 55.6%), with topical vs. oral finasteride, there is less likelihood of systemic adverse reactions of a sexual nature related to a decrease in DHT with topical finasteride.

claims.statement: In the only head-to-head randomized trial, oral minoxidil 5 mg once daily did NOT beat topical minoxidil 5% twice daily over 24 weeks in men. Oral won on one secondary photographic endpoint (vertex) and cost 49% hypertrichosis and 14% headache. The common claim that oral minoxidil is simply stronger than topical is not supported by this trial.
claims.dose: Oral minoxidil 5 mg once daily versus topical minoxidil 5%, 1 mL twice daily, for 24 weeks
claims.population: 90 enrolled / 68 completing Brazilian men aged 18-55 with Norwood-Hamilton 3V, 4V or 5V AGA, at a single specialist clinic. Mean age 36.6. Small, single-centre, and only 24 weeks.
claims.quote: According to the photographic analysis, oral minoxidil was superior to topical minoxidil on the vertex (24%; 95% CI, 0 to 48; P = .04) but not on the frontal scalp (12%; 95% CI, -12 to 36; P = .24). The most common adverse effects in the oral minoxidil group were hypertrichosis (22 of 45 [49%]) and headache (6 of 45 [14%]). ... In this study, oral minoxidil, 5 mg, once per day for 24 weeks did not demonstrate superiority over topical minoxidil, 5%, twice per day in men with AGA.

claims.statement: The largest low-dose oral minoxidil safety dataset — 1404 patients, two-thirds women — found hypertrichosis in 15.1% and systemic effects (lightheadedness 1.7%, fluid retention 1.3%, tachycardia 0.9%) that were infrequent, with no life-threatening events. This is reassuring but it is retrospective with no control group, so background rates for these symptoms are unknown.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: the abstract states doses were titrated in 1065 of 1404 patients but does not report the dose range, so no specific mg figure can be attached to this safety profile
claims.population: 1404 patients (943 women, 461 men), mean age 43, range 8-86, treated at least 3 months for any type of alopecia across multiple international centres. Includes children and elderly people.
claims.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
claims.quote: The most frequent adverse effect was hypertrichosis (15.1%), which led to treatment withdrawal in 14 patients (0.5%). Systemic adverse effects included lightheadedness (1.7%), fluid retention (1.3%), tachycardia (0.9%), headache (0.4%), periorbital edema (0.3%), and insomnia (0.2%), leading to drug discontinuation in 29 patients (1.2%). No life-threatening adverse effects were observed. Retrospective design and lack of a control group.

claims.statement: The current expert-consensus starting doses for low-dose oral minoxidil are 1.25 mg/day for women (range 0.625-5 mg/day) and 2.5 mg/day for men (range 1.25-5 mg/day). Named contraindications are pericardial disease, uncontrolled hypertension and pregnancy. These are consensus numbers from a Delphi panel, not doses established by a dose-ranging trial.
claims.dose: Women: 1.25 mg/day starting, 0.625-5 mg/day range. Men: 2.5 mg/day starting, 1.25-5 mg/day range.
claims.population: Adults with hair loss disorders, as judged by an international panel of hair-loss specialist dermatologists. Lower doses advised for adolescents; caution in renal or hepatic impairment.
claims.quote: Common adverse effects include dose-dependent hypertrichosis (24% incidence), transient shedding (16-22%), and mild peripheral edema (2%), while serious complications, including pericardial effusion, are rare at doses used for alopecia. International Delphi consensus supports standardized dosing: 1.25 mg/day starting dose for women (range 0.625-5 mg/day) and 2.5 mg/day for men (range 1.25-5 mg/day), with lower doses recommended for adolescents and caution advised in renal/hepatic impairment. Contraindications include pericardial disease, uncontrolled hypertension, and pregnancy.

claims.statement: In women, the evidence splits sharply by drug. Topical minoxidil works for female pattern hair loss (and 2% is not inferior to 5%). Finasteride 1 mg did NOT beat placebo in women across three trials — 30/67 improved on finasteride versus 33/70 on placebo. Extrapolating men's finasteride results to women is not supported.
claims.dose: Finasteride 1 mg/day; topical minoxidil 2% or 5%
claims.population: 47 trials, 5290 participants with female pattern hair loss. Only 5 of 47 trials were at low risk of bias; the finasteride evidence was graded low quality.
claims.quote: Three studies investigated finasteride 1 mg compared to placebo. In the finasteride group 30/67 participants experienced improvement compared to 33/70 in the placebo group (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.37; low quality evidence). ... there was evidence to support the efficacy and safety of topical minoxidil in the treatment of FPHL (mainly moderate to low quality evidence). Furthermore, there was no difference in effect between the minoxidil 2% and 5% with the quality of evidence rated moderate to low for most outcomes. Finasteride was no more effective than placebo (low quality evidence).

claims.statement: In a one-year randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy men, dutasteride suppressed DHT 94% and finasteride 5 mg suppressed it 73%. Both cut total sperm count significantly at 26 weeks (dutasteride -28.6%, finasteride -34.3%) but not at 52 weeks or 24 weeks after stopping; sperm motility fell 6-12% and had not recovered at follow-up. Effects were called mild and apparently reversible — but this used finasteride 5 mg, not the 1 mg hair-loss dose.
claims.dose: Dutasteride 0.5 mg/day or finasteride 5 mg/day for 1 year
claims.population: 99 healthy men randomized (dutasteride 33, finasteride 34, placebo 32). Healthy volunteers, not men with fertility problems — and not men on the 1 mg finasteride dose.
claims.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
claims.quote: D and F significantly (P < 0.001) suppressed serum DHT, compared with placebo (D, 94%; F, 73%) and transiently increased serum T. In both treatment groups, total sperm count, compared with baseline, was significantly decreased at 26 wk (D, -28.6%; F, -34.3%) but not at 52 wk (D, -24.9%; F, -16.2%) or the 24-wk follow-up (D, -23.3%; F, -6.2%). ... There was a significant reduction of -6 to 12% in sperm motility during treatment with both D and F and at follow-up.

claims.statement: DOCUMENTED SIDE OF THE PFS DEBATE: in a prospective follow-up of 54 men who had already reported sexual side effects persisting at least 3 months after stopping finasteride, 96% were still symptomatic at a mean of 14 months later, and 89% met the ASEX definition of sexual dysfunction. Neither duration of finasteride use nor duration of symptoms predicted improvement. This establishes that in men who report persistence, symptoms often do not resolve — it does NOT establish how often persistence occurs, because there is no denominator and no control group.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: subjects had taken finasteride for male pattern hair loss (typically 1 mg/day) but the abstract does not state doses; the study is about the post-discontinuation state, not a dose
claims.population: 54 otherwise healthy young men, self-selected/referred because they already had persistent symptoms, with no baseline sexual dysfunction, medical or psychiatric conditions, or other prescription medication before finasteride. A symptomatic cohort, not a random sample of finasteride users.
claims.quote: Subjects (N = 54) with persistent sexual side effects associated with finasteride were reassessed after 9-16 months (mean 14 months). All subjects were otherwise healthy young men without any baseline sexual dysfunction, medical conditions, psychiatric conditions, or use of oral prescription medications prior to taking finasteride for male pattern hair loss. ... At reassessment persistent sexual side effects continued to be present in 96% of subjects. According to the ASEX scores, 89% of subjects met the definition of sexual dysfunction. Neither the length of finasteride use nor the duration of the sexual side effects correlated to changes in scores of sexual dysfunction.

claims.statement: CONTESTED SIDE: a network meta-analysis of the randomized trials of finasteride 1 mg, finasteride 5 mg and dutasteride 0.5 mg found the active drugs were not significantly different from placebo in eliciting global sexual dysfunction. The randomized evidence base does not show a signal that the case-series literature reports.
claims.dose: Finasteride 1 mg/day, finasteride 5 mg/day, dutasteride 0.5 mg/day
claims.population: Men in randomized controlled trials of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors for androgenetic alopecia. Trial durations are short (mostly 24-48 weeks) and none were designed to detect symptoms persisting after discontinuation.
claims.quote: The active interventions were not significantly different than each other in efficacy and were not significantly different from placebo in eliciting sexual dysfunction. Benefit-risk analysis resulted in an arbitrary ranking due to the lack of statistically significant difference between active treatments.

claims.statement: Pharmacovigilance sits between the two positions. In WHO VigiBase, finasteride carried a significant disproportionality signal for suicidality (ROR 1.63) and psychological adverse events (ROR 4.33), concentrated in men under 45 taking it for alopecia (ROR 3.47) and absent in older BPH patients. But reports rose sharply after 2012 (ROR 2.13), and the authors themselves attribute the signal to stimulated reporting and/or genuine vulnerability in younger patients — disproportionality is a reporting metric, not an incidence rate.
claims.dose: prescriber-led: spontaneous reports, doses not captured; the alopecia-indication subgroup implies finasteride 1 mg/day
claims.population: 3282 adverse events of interest among finasteride users in VigiBase (3206 male, 98.9%); 615 of 868 with age data were 18-44. Spontaneous reports, subject to reporting bias and media effects.
claims.quote: A significant disproportionality signal for suicidality (ROR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.47-1.81) and psychological adverse events (ROR, 4.33; 95% CI, 4.17-4.49) in finasteride was identified. In sensitivity analyses, younger patients (ROR, 3.47; 95% CI, 2.90-4.15) and those with alopecia (ROR, 2.06; 95% CI, 1.81-2.34) had significant disproportionality signals for increased suicidality; such signals were not detected in older patients with BPH. Sensitivity analyses also showed that the reports of these adverse events significantly increased after 2012 (ROR, 2.13; 95% CI, 1.91-2.39).

claims.statement: How the specialists who prescribe these drugs see it: in a 2026 survey of 54 Spanish hair and nail dermatologists, 83.3% had never encountered a case of post-finasteride syndrome, 98.1% considered it psychiatric in origin, 92.6% believed 5-ARI adverse effects are reversible on discontinuation — and 90.7% agreed the current scientific evidence on PFS is poor. That last figure is the honest common ground: both camps agree the evidence is weak.
claims.dose: none — a survey of clinician opinion, not a dosing or outcome study
claims.population: 54 dermatologists in the Spanish Hair and Nail Disorders Group. This is expert opinion about patients, not patient data; specialists may see a different case mix than the online communities where PFS is most reported.
claims.quote: A total of 83.3% of respondents had never encountered cases of PFS in their clinical practice. Most participants (98.1%) considered that PFS has a psychiatric origin, and 92.6% believed that any adverse effect of 5-ARIs is reversible after treatment discontinuation. ... Consensus was reached for 13 of the 15 items, with 90.7% agreeing that current scientific evidence on PFS is poor and 85.1% identifying a specific patient profile (young men with pre-existing anxiety or depression). ... high-quality longitudinal studies are needed to establish clear guidelines for its diagnosis and management.

claims.statement: Patellar tendinopathy isometric stage, fully specified: 5 repetitions of a 45-second single-leg isometric hold at 70% of maximum voluntary contraction, performed at 60 degrees of knee flexion on a leg press or leg extension, daily. This is the most completely reported isometric prescription in a positive randomised trial.
claims.dose: 5 reps x 45 s hold; 60 degrees knee flexion; 70% MVC; single-leg leg press or leg extension; daily
claims.population: 76 athletes aged 18-35 with ultrasound-confirmed patellar tendinopathy, VISA-P <80, playing sport at least 3x/week; mean age 24, 76% male, median symptom duration 2 years. Predominantly young male jumping athletes — not a general adult population.
claims.quote: stage 1 consisted of daily isometric exercises (single-leg leg-press or leg-extension, 5 repetitions of 45 s mid-range (60° knee flexion) quadriceps isometric hold at 70% of maximum voluntary contraction)

claims.statement: The isotonic stage of the same protocol progressed from 4 sets of 15 reps in a restricted mid-range (10-60 degrees knee flexion) to 4 sets of 6 reps at higher load through a fuller range (near-full extension to 90 degrees), performed every second day, alternating with the isometric day.
claims.dose: 4 sets x 15 reps at 10-60 degrees, progressing to 4 sets x 6 reps at near-full extension to 90 degrees; every second day
claims.population: Same 38 patients randomised to progressive tendon-loading exercise; young athletes with chronic patellar tendinopathy. Range-of-motion restriction early is a deliberate load-limiting device, not an arbitrary detail.
claims.quote: The isotonic exercises were also performed as a single-leg leg-press or leg-extension, and started with 4 sets of 15 repetitions between 10° and 60° of knee flexion and slowly progressed to 4 sets of 6 repetitions with increasing load and knee angles between almost full extension and 90° flexion.

claims.statement: THE NUMERIC PAIN-MONITORING RULE, with its source: progression was gated on a single-leg squat used as a standardised pain provocation test. If that squat produced VAS 3 or less on 0-10, and the current stage had been performed for at least one week, the athlete advanced. This is the ≤3/10 rule that most modern tendon protocols cite.
claims.dose: Provocation test = one single-leg squat; threshold = VAS ≤3/10; minimum 1 week per stage before advancing
claims.population: Patellar tendinopathy, 18-35, ultrasound-confirmed. The rule was applied to exercise progression AND to return to sport and general athletic activity in the same trial.
claims.quote: Progression to each subsequent stage was defined using individualised progression criteria, based on the level of pain experienced during a pain provocation test that consisted of one single-leg squat. If the VAS-score was 3 or less and exercises of the stage were performed for at least 1 week, progression to the next stage was advised.

claims.statement: The staged, pain-limited protocol beat the traditional pain-provoking eccentric decline squat by 9 VISA-P points at 24 weeks. Notably, the comparator arm was deliberately instructed to work AT VAS 5 or above — so this is a direct test of loading into pain versus loading under a pain ceiling, and the ceiling won.
claims.dose: Comparator: eccentric decline squat on 25-degree board, twice daily, 12 weeks, instructed to reach VAS ≥5/10 during exercise
claims.population: 76 athletes with mostly chronic patellar tendinopathy (median 2 years), 82% of whom had already failed prior treatment.
claims.quote: The improvement in VISA-P score was significantly better for PTLE than for EET after 24 weeks (28 vs 18 points, adjusted mean between-group difference, 9 (95% CI 1 to 16); p=0.023). ... Patients were instructed to perform the exercises with pain (VAS score ≥5 points on a scale 0–10 during the exercises).

claims.statement: The second, older numeric rule (the Silbernagel pain-monitoring model) uses a HIGHER ceiling than the ≤3/10 rule: load is added when pain does not exceed 5/10, and tendon-loading sport is permitted provided pain stays at or below 50/100 mm AND subsides within 24 hours. The 24-hour resolution criterion is the part most often dropped when people quote this rule.
claims.dose: Add load (5 kg increments) when pain ≤5 on 0-10 NRS; resume loading sport if pain ≤50 mm on 0-100 mm VAS and it subsides within 24 h
claims.population: Protocol description for recreational athletes aged 18-60 with chronic (≥3 months) unilateral midportion Achilles tendinopathy. The rule originates in Achilles work and is applied to patellar and elbow tendons by convention, not by trial.
claims.quote: Progression is made by changing from bipedal to unipedal exercises, by progressing from concentric-eccentric to purely eccentric loading, by adding weight in a backpack (in steps of 5 kg when pain did not exceed 5 on a 0–10 numerical rating scale), and finally by using fast-rebounding and plyometric exercises. ... they are allowed to resume tendon loading sports activities, as long as pain does not exceed 50 mm on a 0–100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS), and pain subsides within 24 h after the activity.

claims.statement: The evidence that you can keep training on a symptomatic tendon: an RCT randomised patients to continue running and jumping under the pain-monitoring model versus stopping those activities for 6 weeks. Continuing was not worse. This is the trial behind 'you do not have to rest it'.
claims.dose: Continued running/jumping under pain-monitoring model vs 6 weeks cessation; identical rehab programme in both arms
claims.population: 38 patients with Achilles tendinopathy (19 per arm). Achilles, not patellar or elbow — the transfer to elbow tendons is an assumption, not a finding.
claims.quote: The exercise training group (n = 19) was allowed, with the use of a pain-monitoring model, to continue Achilles tendon-loading activity, such as running and jumping, whereas the active rest group (n = 19) had to stop such activities during the first 6 weeks. ... No negative effects could be demonstrated from continuing Achilles tendon-loading activity, such as running and jumping, with the use of a pain-monitoring model, during treatment.
claims.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine

claims.statement: HONEST CAVEAT ON THE PAIN RULE ITSELF: a systematic review of 30 RCTs found pain-based progression criteria dominate the literature but are not backed by strong evidence, and no trial has yet compared the same exercise programme run under different pain thresholds. The ≤3/10 and ≤5/10 numbers are conventions that happened to be used in trials that worked — they are not validated cut-points.
claims.dose: none
claims.population: 30 RCTs of midportion Achilles, patellar or gluteal tendinopathy with progressive exercise as monotherapy. Lower limb only; elbow tendons were not reviewed.
claims.quote: There is a predominant use of pain-based criteria, but the utilisation of these criteria is not supported by strong evidence. This review evidences the need for studies that compare the same exercise programme using different progression criteria.

claims.statement: Heavy slow resistance for the patellar tendon, fully specified: 3 sessions per week; three bilateral movements (squat, leg press, Bulgarian split squat); load stepped 12RM (weeks 1-2) to 10RM (3-4) to 8RM (5-6) to 6RM (7-8); tempo enforced by metronome at 3 s eccentric plus 3 s concentric, 6 s per repetition; 4 sets per movement with 2 minutes rest.
claims.dose: 3x/week; 12RM→10RM→8RM→6RM over 8 weeks; 3 s eccentric + 3 s concentric (6 s/rep); 4 sets; 2 min rest; >70% 1RM, no more than 12 reps/set
claims.population: 51 college students aged 18-24 with chronic (>3 months) patellar tendinopathy at a Chinese sports university, VISA-P <80, ultrasound-confirmed. Almost entirely male (46/51). The 4 sets and 2 min rest are stated in the combined-therapy paragraph, which explicitly states that group followed the same regimen as the HSR group.
claims.quote: Subjects were asked to perform three weekly training sessions, each including three movements (squat, leg press, Bulgarian deep squat). ... Load intensity and repetitions were progressively adjusted throughout the program: starting with 12 repetitions maximum (12RM) in the first two weeks, reducing to 10RM in the third and fourth, 8RM in the fifth and sixth, and finally 6RM in the seventh and eighth weeks. During each exercise, subjects followed a metronome, spending 3 s on both the eccentric and concentric phases of the movement, totaling 6 s per movement. ... Participants performed four sets of each maneuver, taking a 2-minute rest between sets.

claims.statement: That same HSR trial used a slightly different numeric rule from Breda's: pain under VAS 3 during a session was acceptable provided it did not INCREASE session to session. The between-session trend, not the within-session number, was the stop signal.
claims.dose: Continue if VAS <3 and pain does not increase in subsequent sessions
claims.population: College-age athletes with chronic patellar tendinopathy under direct therapist supervision every session — a much more supervised setting than self-management.
claims.quote: Participants with partial pain (VAS < 3) were allowed to continue as long as pain did not increase in subsequent sessions.

claims.statement: The foundational HSR trial: 12 weeks of HSR matched eccentric decline squats and beat corticosteroid injection in the long run. Corticosteroid looked good short-term then deteriorated; HSR held its gains at 6 months and produced measurable tendon change (reduced swelling and vascularisation, elevated collagen turnover).
claims.dose: 12 weeks; HSR vs eccentric decline squat vs peritendinous corticosteroid injection
claims.population: 39 MALE patients with patellar tendinopathy. All male — no female data in this trial at all.
claims.quote: Thirty-nine male patients were randomized to CORT, ECC or HSR for 12 weeks. ... VISA-p and VAS improvements were maintained at follow-up in ECC and HSR but deteriorated in CORT (P<0.05). ... HSR has good short- and long-term clinical effects accompanied by pathology improvement and increased collagen turnover.
claims.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports

claims.statement: ISOMETRIC ANALGESIA, THE ORIGINAL POSITIVE RESULT: a single bout dropped decline-squat pain from 7.0/10 to 0.17/10 and held the reduction for 45 minutes, with a parallel drop in cortical inhibition. This near-total abolition of pain is the number that made isometrics famous — and it came from six volleyball players.
claims.dose: Single bout of isometric quadriceps contractions vs isotonic; outcomes at 0 and 45 min
claims.population: SIX volleyball players with patellar tendinopathy, single-blinded crossover. n=6. This is the entire evidence base for the headline effect size.
claims.quote: 6 volleyball players with PT participated. Condition effects were detected with greater pain relief immediately from isometric contractions: isometric contractions reduced SLDS (mean±SD) from 7.0±2.04 to 0.17±0.41, and isotonic contractions reduced SLDS (mean±SD) from 6.33±2.80 to 3.75±3.28 (p<0.001).

claims.statement: The in-season isometric protocol with its parameters: leg-extension isometric holds at 60 degrees knee flexion at 80% MVIC, 4 sessions per week for 4 weeks, versus isotonic leg extension at 80% of 8RM with time-under-load matched. Isometrics produced greater immediate analgesia across the 4 weeks. Note the intensity here is 80% MVIC, not the 70% used by Breda.
claims.dose: Isometric leg extension holds, 60 degrees knee flexion, 80% MVIC, 4x/week for 4 weeks (time under load and inter-set rest matched to isotonic comparator at 80% of 8RM)
claims.population: 20 in-season jumping athletes (18 men, mean 22.5 years) with clinically diagnosed patellar tendinopathy, training/competing 3x/week. Baseline median pain only 5/10 — a milder group than Rio 2015.
claims.quote: Two quadriceps resistance protocols were compared; (1) isometric leg extension holds at 60 degrees knee flexion (80% of their maximal voluntary isometric contraction) or (2) isotonic leg extension (at 80% of their 8 repetition maximum) 4 times per week for 4 weeks. Time under load and rest between sets was matched between groups. ... Isometric contractions produced significantly greater immediate analgesia (P < 0.002).

claims.statement: REPLICATION FAILURE 1: an independent, pre-registered crossover trial in 21 patients found the pain reduction after isometric exercise was 0.9 points on 0-10 — not 6.8 — was gone by 45 minutes, and was no different from dynamic exercise. The authors concluded contraction mode may not be what matters.
claims.dose: Single session high-load isometric vs dynamic resistance exercise, 7-day washout; outcomes pre, immediately post, 45 min post
claims.population: 21 participants with patellar tendinopathy, Denmark. Pre-registered, participants blinded to hypothesis — methodologically stronger than the original.
claims.quote: There was a significant decrease in pain NRS scores (mean reduction 0.9, NRS 95%CI 0.1-1.7; p = 0.028), and increase in PPTs at the tibialis anterior muscle (mean increase 34 kPa 95%CI 9.5-58.5; p = 0.009) immediately post-exercise. These were not sustained 45 min post-exercise for pain (NRS) or PPTs (p > 0.05). There were no differences between exercise on any outcome.
claims.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport

claims.statement: REPLICATION FAILURE 2: from the same research group as the original, a 4-week in-season trial found isometric and isotonic programmes both reduced pain, with no significant difference between them. Both worked; the isometric advantage did not appear.
claims.dose: 4 isometric or isotonic sessions per week for 4 weeks
claims.population: 29 jumping athletes with patellar tendinopathy playing at least 3x/week, with no modification of training or competition load.
claims.quote: There was no significant difference in NRS pain score change (U=29.0, p=0.208, r=0.29) between the isometric group (median (IQR), 2.5 (1-4.5)) and isotonic group (median (IQR), 3.0 (2-6)).
claims.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport

claims.statement: REPLICATION FAILURE 3, the systematic review: across 13 studies and 346 participants with local musculoskeletal pain, there was no consistent evidence that isometric exercise produces hypoalgesia, and no consistent superiority over comparison interventions. This contrasts with healthy people, where the effect IS consistent. Isometrics are well tolerated — that is the defensible claim, not that they reliably kill pain.
claims.dose: none — review of heterogeneous isometric doses, which the authors flag as a likely reason for the inconsistency
claims.population: 346 participants across 13 randomised and crossover trials in people with localised musculoskeletal symptoms, upper and lower limb.
claims.quote: There was no consistent evidence for EIH following isometric exercise in people with musculoskeletal pain. These findings are different to those reported in asymptomatic populations (where EIH is consistently demonstrated) as well as conditions associated with widespread symptoms such as fibromyalgia (where isometric exercise may induce hyperalgesia). Although well tolerated when prescribed, isometric exercise did not induce EIH consistently for people seeking care for local musculoskeletal symptoms.

claims.statement: ELBOW, AND THE MOST ACTIONABLE FINDING HERE: isometric wrist extension at 10 x 15 s was tested at an intensity 20% BELOW versus 20% ABOVE each person's own pain threshold. Above threshold, pain was HIGHER immediately after and still higher 30 minutes later. Below threshold, it was no different from doing nothing. Pressure pain threshold and pain-free grip did not improve in either condition. At the elbow, pushing an isometric into pain makes it worse.
claims.dose: 10 x 15 s isometric wrist extension; load set 20% below or 20% above individual pain threshold
claims.population: 24 individuals with unilateral chronic lateral epicondylalgia, median 3-month duration, middle-aged. Randomised order, blinded examiner.
claims.quote: Participants performed 3 experimental tasks completed in a randomized order on separate days: control (no exercise) and isometric wrist extension (10×15 s) at load 20% below (infrathreshold), and 20% above (suprathreshold) an individual's pain threshold. ... Individuals with lateral epicondylalgia demonstrated increased pain intensity after an acute bout of isometric exercise performed at an intensity above, but not below, their individual pain threshold.

claims.statement: Eight weeks of daily unsupervised progressive isometric exercise for lateral elbow tendinopathy beat wait-and-see on only one of three primary outcomes. Pain-free grip strength and global rating of change were no better than doing nothing. The authors' own conclusion is that isometrics as a sole treatment are of doubtful efficacy at the elbow.
claims.dose: Single supervised instruction session, then 8 weeks of daily unsupervised progressive isometric exercise
claims.population: 40 adults with unilateral lateral elbow tendinopathy of at least 6 weeks duration (21 exercise, 19 wait-and-see); 98% completed. General clinical population, not athletes.
claims.quote: No group differences were found for success on global rating of change (29% exercise vs 26% wait-and-see (risk difference, 2.3%; 95% CI, -24.5 to 29.1)), or pain-free grip strength (SMD, -0.33; 95% CI, -0.97 to 0.30). ... With only one of the three primary outcomes being significantly different after isometric exercises, it is doubtful if this form of exercise is efficacious as a sole treatment.
claims.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise

claims.statement: For lateral elbow tendinopathy, 12 weeks of home-based heavy slow resistance with elastic bands improved symptoms short and long term, and adding either a corticosteroid injection or tendon needling added nothing. Corticosteroid actually made patient-reported outcomes WORSE at 52 weeks than loading alone.
claims.dose: 12 weeks home-based HSR with elastic band exercises; follow-up at 12, 26 and 52 weeks (primary endpoint 52 weeks)
claims.population: 60 patients with chronic unilateral lateral elbow tendinopathy, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled. Improvements were ~20 DASH points and ~2.5 NRS points across all arms.
claims.quote: These results suggest that 12 weeks of HSR improved symptoms in both the short and the long term and that a CSI or TN did not amplify this effect. In addition, a CSI seemed to impair patient-reported outcomes compared with HSR alone at long-term follow-up.
claims.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine

claims.statement: TOLERABILITY WARNING FOR HEAVY ELBOW LOADING: in a feasibility RCT, a 12-week HSR programme (36 sessions; a wrist flexion/extension exercise plus a forearm pronation/supination exercise with a dumbbell) was completed by only 6 of 19 participants — 32% — mainly because it aggravated pain. The investigators concluded HSR was not suitable for this population. Heavy loading that the patellar tendon tolerates, the common extensor origin often does not.
claims.dose: 12-week home programme, 36 sessions, 2 exercises: wrist extension/flexion, and forearm pronation/supination with a dumbbell; plus extensor stretching 3x/day, 3 sets of 30 s
claims.population: Secondary-care tennis elbow patients at Oslo University Hospital (n=19 in the HSR arm of 60 randomised). Secondary care means a more refractory group than typical gym-goers.
claims.quote: Only 6 of 19 (32%) did comply with heavy slow resistance training. ... Participants had low compliance with heavy slow resistance training mainly due to pain aggravation, which suggests that this intervention was not suitable for patients with tennis elbow.

claims.statement: DISTAL BICEPS — WHICH MOVEMENTS LOAD ELBOW FLEXORS MOST: in a direct EMG comparison of curl grips at 8RM, biceps brachii excitation was 19% higher with a supinated grip than pronated and 12% higher than neutral; brachioradialis was also highest supinated. So supinated curls load the elbow flexors most; pronated (reverse) and neutral (hammer) curls load biceps brachii least while shifting work to anterior deltoid.
claims.dose: Bilateral biceps curl, non-exhaustive 6-rep sets at 8RM, supinated vs pronated vs neutral forearm
claims.population: TEN competitive bodybuilders, healthy, surface EMG. No tendinopathy patients; EMG amplitude is a proxy for muscle drive, NOT a measurement of distal biceps tendon force.
claims.quote: During the ascending phase, (i) biceps brachii excitation was greater with the supinated compared to the pronated [+19(7)%, ES: 2.60] and neutral handgrip [+12(9)%, ES: 1.24], (ii) the brachioradialis showed greater excitation with the supinated compared to the pronated [+5(4)%, ES: 1.01] and neutral handgrip [+6(5)%, ES: 1.10]

claims.statement: COUNTERINTUITIVE FINDING FOR PULL-UPS: across supinated (chin-up), pronated, neutral and rope grips, arm and forearm muscle activation over a complete repetition was SIMILAR — switching to a pronated grip does not meaningfully unload the biceps in a pull-up. What did differ was phase: biceps brachii and brachioradialis activation was significantly HIGHER in the concentric than the eccentric phase, so the lowering portion is where elbow-flexor drive is lowest.
claims.dose: Bodyweight pull-ups, four grip variations, surface EMG of eight shoulder-arm-forearm muscles normalised to %MVIC
claims.population: 19 strength-trained males, mean age 24.9, healthy. Not tendinopathy patients. Again, EMG amplitude is not tendon load.
claims.quote: The concentric phases of each pull-up variation resulted in significantly greater EMGARV of the brachioradialis, biceps brachii, and pectoralis major in comparison to the eccentric phases (P=<0.01). Results indicate that EMGPEAK and EMGARV of the shoulder-arm-forearm complex during complete repetitions of pull-up variants are similar despite varying hand orientations

claims.statement: Same pattern in the lat pulldown: pronating the grip increased latissimus dorsi activity but had NO effect on biceps brachii, at either wide or narrow grip. Switching from an underhand to an overhand pulldown will not spare the elbow flexors.
claims.dose: Anterior lat pulldown at 70% 1RM, 5 reps, 2 s concentric and 2 s eccentric cadence; wide (carrying width) and narrow (biacromial) grips, pronated and supinated
claims.population: 12 healthy men. Healthy, no elbow symptoms; single session EMG.
claims.quote: Repeated-measures analysis of variance for each muscle revealed that a pronated grip elicited greater LD activity than a supinated grip (p < 0.05), but had no influence of grip type on the MT and BB muscles.
claims.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.statement: GRIP AIDS, PART 1 — THICK GRIPS DO CHANGE RECRUITMENT, AND IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS FOR A DISTAL BICEPS: adding fat-grip attachments significantly INCREASED forearm muscle activation and significantly DECREASED upper-arm (biceps and triceps) activation during deadlift, bent-over row and pull-ups, while cutting 1RM in every exercise and reducing pull-up reps. Upright row and concentration curl showed no change.
claims.dose: Fat Gripz attached to Olympic barbell vs bare bar; 1RM testing in deadlift, bent-over row, upright row, concentration curl; max pull-ups
claims.population: 15 resistance-trained men, mean age 22.4, healthy. Acute single-session EMG and 1RM; no tendinopathy patients and no tendon-load measurement.
claims.quote: When using the FG, 1RM strength was significantly decreased for each exercise, and the maximal number of pull-ups completed was significantly lower. Electromyography muscle activity was significantly increased in the forearm and shoulder muscles, but significantly decreased in the upper arm muscles with the use of FG during deadlift, bent-over row, and pull-ups. However, there were no differences for EMG activity for upright row and concentration curl.
claims.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.statement: GRIP AIDS, PART 2 — LIFTING STRAPS: in the only strap EMG trial retrieved, straps changed nothing in the lat pulldown — not 1RM, not reps to failure at 70% 1RM, not latissimus dorsi activation. IMPORTANT LIMITATION: this study measured latissimus dorsi only. It did NOT measure biceps brachii or forearm flexors, so it cannot answer whether straps offload the elbow flexors. That question is untested.
claims.dose: Lat pulldown, 3 sets to concentric failure at 70% 1RM, 60 s rest, with vs without lifting straps; plus 1RM test
claims.population: 12 resistance-trained men, mean 6.6 years training experience, healthy. Crossover. Only latissimus dorsi EMG reported.
claims.quote: There were no differences between the WS and WOS conditions in the number of repetitions per set, total repetitions and latissimus dorsi muscle activation. In conclusion, the findings of this study demonstrate that the use of lifting straps in the lat pull-down exercise by resistance-trained individuals does not promote beneficial effect in the 1RM value, the number of repetitions performed with 70% of 1RM, and muscle activation.

claims.statement: THE HONEST BASELINE FOR DISTAL BICEPS: distal biceps tendinopathy is very rare and there is limited published evidence on it. Everything above about elbow-flexor loading is extrapolation — there is no loading protocol trial for this tendon. The review also flags that tendinopathy here can progress to rupture, which is why it should not be self-managed by simply training through it.
claims.dose: none — no protocol exists
claims.population: Narrative review of medial elbow, distal biceps and distal triceps tendinopathy. Explicitly a scarcity-of-evidence review, not a trial.
claims.quote: Distal biceps and triceps tendinopathies are very rare and there is limited evidence published. Sequelae of tendinopathy include tendon rupture and so it is vital to manage these tendinopathies appropriately in order to minimise this significant complication.

claims.statement: Arthroscopic subacromial decompression was no better than placebo (arthroscopy-only) surgery for shoulder pain and function at 6 months; both surgical arms beat no treatment by an amount the investigators judged not clinically important.
claims.dose: none - surgical trial; no exercise or drug dose applies
claims.population: 313 UK adults with subacromial pain for at least 3 months, intact rotator cuff tendons, who had ALREADY completed a non-operative programme including exercise therapy and at least one steroid injection - i.e. the failed-conservative-care group, not a first-presentation lifter
claims.quote: Mean Oxford Shoulder Score did not differ between the two surgical groups at 6 months (decompression mean 32·7 points [SD 11·6] vs arthroscopy mean 34·2 points [9·2]; mean difference -1·3 points (95% CI -3·9 to 1·3, p=0·3141). Both surgical groups showed a small benefit over no treatment (mean 29·4 points [SD 11·9], mean difference vs decompression 2·8 points [95% CI 0·5-5·2], p=0·0186; mean difference vs arthroscopy 4·2 [1·8-6·6], p=0·0014) but these differences were not clinically important.

claims.statement: In a double-blind sham-surgery trial, subacromial decompression gave no benefit over diagnostic arthroscopy at 24 months. The trial's own authors warn that the apparent edge of surgery over exercise therapy in that trial is biased in surgery's favour.
claims.dose: none - surgical trial; minimal clinically important difference prespecified at 15 points on a 0-100 VAS
claims.population: 210 patients in three Finnish public hospitals with symptoms consistent with shoulder impingement syndrome, two-year follow-up
claims.quote: In this controlled trial involving patients with a shoulder impingement syndrome, arthroscopic subacromial decompression provided no benefit over diagnostic arthroscopy at 24 months. ...
